process.title: Send the last marked script
process.description: Before anything is booked, send the most recent marked Arabic A paper, the school's criterion marks if they were given, and the next deadline. If the family does not know whether the course is Literature or Language and Literature, the script usually answers it.

process.description: The trial is spent re-marking that script against criteria A to D and comparing the result with the school's. The output is four numbers and a named starting point, which the family keeps whether or not they continue. The free trial carries no card requirement.

process.description: HL essay first, oral first, or Paper 1 technique first - the order depends on which deadline is nearest and which criterion is lowest, not on the syllabus sequence. We write the order down with the dates attached so it can be checked later.

process.description: Sessions run live online in Gulf Standard Time, usually after 18:00 on a Dubai weekday. Every second week the student produces one timed piece, which is marked criterion by criterion and becomes the material for the next two sessions.

process.description: Four marked pieces in, the family and the tutor look at the criterion history together. If a criterion has not moved, the plan changes. If the match is wrong, we rematch rather than persist, and the record transfers to the new tutor.

whyPoints.title: Arabic A, not Arabic generally
whyPoints.description: Most Arabic tutoring available in Dubai is pitched at Arabic B or at school Arabic. Arabic A Literature at HL needs someone who can mark a comparative essay in fusha against criteria A to D and justify each number. That is the specialism we match for.

whyPoints.title: Dialect interference treated as a named list
whyPoints.description: A fluent speaker losing criterion D marks does not need beginner grammar. They need their own twelve to twenty recurring slips written down and checked before submission. The list comes from their scripts, so it is specific to them and it shortens.

whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, reads drafts and responds to them against criteria. A tutor does not write, redraft or finish an HL essay, Extended Essay, TOK essay or any assessed component. Saying so before the first session is how we keep it from becoming a negotiation at a deadline.

whyPoints.title: A record that survives the tutor
whyPoints.description: Marked scripts are screen-shared and kept, drafts are dated, criterion marks go into a running table. If the tutor changes, the history does not reset, and a parent can see two years of movement rather than remembering a sequence of impressions.

faqs.question: What does an IB DP Arabic A home tutor in Dubai actually cost?
faqs.answer: Dubai market rates for qualified online subject tutors run roughly AED 150-300 an hour, with IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200-450 and premium named tutors above AED 500, according to published rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table. In-home visits sit at AED 180-500 because travel is priced inside the hour. Those are market figures, not ours. IB Gram starts with a free trial lesson and a consultation, and quotes against level, component and session length rather than from a tier list, because Arabic A HL essay supervision and weekly Paper 1 practice are different pieces of work.

faqs.question: Is Arabic A Literature or Arabic A Language and Literature better for my child?
faqs.answer: Neither is stronger; they suit different readers. Literature studies nine works at SL and thirteen at HL, all literary, and rewards sustained close reading. Language and Literature studies four literary works at SL or six at HL alongside non-literary material such as journalism, advertising and political speech, and rewards analysis of how language works in context. A student who reads fiction willingly usually does better in Literature. A student who argues well about media and rhetoric often does better in Language and Literature. In Dubai the practical constraint is usually which one the school timetables, not which one suits.

faqs.question: Can my child take Arabic A if their school does not teach it?
faqs.answer: Often yes. The IB allows Literature SL to be taken school-supported self-taught, where the student reads the nine works independently and the school supervises the Individual Oral. The external papers are identical to the taught course. It is available at Standard Level only, never HL. In Dubai this route matters because several British-curriculum schools run no Arabic A class, which otherwise pushes an Arab first-language student into Arabic B and a course below their reading level. Raise it with the DP coordinator in DP1; it needs school agreement and it needs planning time.

faqs.question: How many marks is the Arabic A Individual Oral worth and how is it structured?
faqs.answer: Fifteen minutes, marked out of 40 across four criteria of 10 marks each. The student speaks for ten minutes on how a global issue is presented in two extracts - one from a work originally written in Arabic, one from a work studied in translation - then answers five minutes of questions. It carries 30% of the Standard Level grade and 20% at Higher Level. Extract selection decides a great deal of the mark before the student opens their mouth, which is why rehearsal starts with choosing extracts that genuinely let the issue be argued rather than ones that are easy to talk about.

faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic fluently but loses marks on written work. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always register rather than ability. Dubai students speak a dialect at home, hear several others at school, and are assessed entirely in Modern Standard Arabic. Spoken verb forms, dialect vocabulary and conversational sentence rhythm reach the page unnoticed because they sound correct to the writer. That lands under criterion D, and a report describing it as weak language is accurate and unhelpful. The fix is a personal error list built from the student's own marked scripts - usually twelve to twenty recurring items - checked before every submission. It is a fortnight of work, not a year.

faqs.question: What is the word limit on the Arabic A HL essay and how much does it count?
faqs.answer: Between 1,200 and 1,500 words, marked out of 20 across four criteria, and worth 20% of the Higher Level grade. It exists only at HL. Because it is written over months rather than in an exam hall, it is the component students postpone, and postponing it means a fifth of the grade lands in the busiest term of DP2. The single most useful session is the first one, where a theme is narrowed into an arguable question. Broad questions invite summary, and summary caps the analysis criterion whatever the quality of the writing that follows.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write my child's Arabic A HL essay?
faqs.answer: No, and any tutor who offers to is a risk to your child's diploma rather than a shortcut. The IB treats work that is not the student's own as malpractice, and the consequence falls on the candidate. What a tutor may legitimately do: help narrow the question, discuss whether the evidence supports the argument, read drafts and respond to them against the published criteria, and teach the conventions of academic writing in Arabic. What a tutor may not do: supply content, write or rewrite passages, edit the prose to completion, or decide the argument. We keep every dated draft so the progression is visibly the student's.

faqs.question: How does the mandatory Arabic requirement in Dubai schools affect Arabic A?
faqs.answer: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools whatever international curriculum the school is licensed for, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies because expectations and language of instruction differ. A DP student taking Arabic A is therefore frequently carrying mandatory provision as well, sometimes with a different teacher and a different report. Knowing which teacher assesses which thing prevents families chasing the wrong feedback. The requirement is a school obligation, not something tutoring satisfies or replaces.

faqs.question: Does taking Arabic A get my child the IB bilingual diploma?
faqs.answer: It can. One route to the bilingual diploma is completing two language A courses and scoring grade 3 or higher in both, which for most Dubai students means Arabic A alongside English A. Other routes exist through studying a sciences or individuals-and-societies subject in a second language, or through an Extended Essay submitted in a second language. The award is made by the IB on the results, not applied for, and your DP coordinator can confirm which route your child's subject choices put them on. It is worth checking in DP1 while the timetable can still change.

faqs.question: Why is an online Arabic A tutor better than one who comes to our villa?
faqs.answer: Because of who is available rather than where the lesson happens. A tutor who travels to your community is drawn from whoever lives within a reasonable drive; Arabic A Literature specialists are thin across the whole emirate, so the overlap in any one area is small. Online delivery removes the radius. It also removes travel from the billed hour, which in Dubai on a weekday evening is a real portion of the session. And a screen-shared script can be annotated and saved, so the marked record accumulates instead of leaving the house with the tutor.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send Arabic tutors to homes in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Arabic A tuition for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, which for most Dubai households means a slot after 18:00 on a weekday or a morning at the weekend. We also hold no UAE office, centre or branch, and claim no permit or accreditation from KHDA, the Ministry of Education or the IB. Any tutor you work with must hold their own MoHRE private tuition work permit.

faqs.question: When should we start Arabic A tutoring if exams are in May?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families do, because two components close before the papers. The Individual Oral is recorded in a school window during DP2 and the HL essay is submitted before that, so by the spring of DP2 up to 40% of an HL grade is already fixed. The most useful entry point is DP1 term two, when the portfolio is forming and the oral works can still be chosen deliberately. Starting six weeks before the session is not pointless - Paper 1 technique responds quickly - but it limits the work to the components still open.

faqs.question: How will I know the tutoring is working rather than just happening?
faqs.answer: By four numbers per piece of work. Every marked piece gets a mark for each of the four criteria, dated, in a running table you can see. After eight weeks that is four pieces and sixteen numbers, and the pattern answers the question. Criterion C rising while A stays flat means the structure teaching landed and the reading work has not begun. Flat marks across eight weeks mean the diagnosis was wrong, the student is not writing between sessions, or the match is poor - and the first two are fixable without changing tutor. We say which one we think it is.

faqs.question: Can sessions move during Ramadan or around school exam weeks?
faqs.answer: Yes, and they usually need to. Ramadan shifts earlier each year and compresses the revision weeks before the session; many Dubai families prefer post-Iftar session times, which online delivery accommodates without a travel calculation. School mock weeks and internal deadline clusters are the other reason to move a slot. The pattern we suggest is to protect the fortnightly marked piece even when the live session moves, because the marked work is what the record is built from. A paused month with no written work leaves a visible gap in the criterion history.

faqs.question: What should we send before the first Arabic A session?
faqs.answer: Three things, and none of them take long to gather. The most recent marked Arabic A script, with the school's criterion marks if they were written on it. The learner portfolio or a list of works studied so far, which also settles whether the course is Literature or Language and Literature. And the next deadline on the subject's calendar, whether that is an oral window, an essay draft or a mock. With those, the trial session can be spent re-marking real work rather than establishing basic facts about the course.

It is a marked script, re-marked against criteria A to D, with the four numbers written down and compared against the school's. Sessions run one-to-one online in Gulf Standard Time. We will tell you if Arabic A is not where your child's marks are actually being lost, because the alternative is billing you for the wrong subject.

intro.heading: Three different students search for the same thing
paragraphs: Arabic A is not one situation. The first student is in a Dubai school that teaches Arabic A properly, in a class of twenty, and is losing marks on written analysis despite speaking Arabic at home every day. The second is in a school that offers no Arabic A at all and wants to sit it as a school-supported self-taught candidate, which is possible but only in one specific configuration. The third is deciding whether to carry Arabic A alongside English A in order to receive a bilingual diploma. Those three need different first sessions, and most pages on this subject answer only the first.

The self-taught route is the one families know least about and the one where a wrong assumption costs the most. Language A: Literature may be taken as school-supported self-taught, at Standard Level only. That means no Higher Level, and it means Literature rather than Language and Literature. The school registers the candidate, provides a supervisor and administrative support, and is not obliged to teach the course. Everything else - reading the works, building the analysis, preparing the individual oral - sits with the student. Which is precisely why these candidates are the ones who most need a subject specialist.

The bilingual diploma question is the other one worth getting right early. Completing two Group 1 languages at grade 3 or above earns it, which is the route most Dubai families have in mind when they ask about Arabic A alongside English A. There is also a second route, which almost nobody mentions: taking a Group 3 or Group 4 subject in a language other than the nominated Language A, with a grade 3 or above in both. That second route changes the arithmetic for some students and is worth checking with the coordinator before a subject choice is locked.

Running underneath all of this in Dubai is a separate requirement that families routinely confuse with Arabic A. Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the international curriculum a school is licensed by KHDA to teach, and KHDA requires that Arab and non-Arab students be taught separately in those subjects, with combined classes prohibited. Those lessons are not Arabic A. They have their own content, their own language of instruction rules and their own teachers, and a student can be doing well in one and badly in the other.

IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. We hold no accreditation from the IB, KHDA, the Ministry of Education or any other authority, we have no UAE office, and we do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE - home visits are a service we offer only in India. Dubai families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time by a named Arabic A specialist, with a free trial lesson before any payment.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic A sits in Group 1 of the Diploma, the studies in language and literature group, and it behaves exactly as any other Language A does. What differs in Dubai is the surrounding arrangement: who teaches it, whether the school offers it at all, and how it sits beside the mandatory Arabic lessons every private school must run.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic A is offered as Literature or as Language and Literature, each at Standard and Higher Level, with the same assessment architecture as the equivalent English A courses: an unseen Paper 1, a comparative Paper 2 written without the texts, an individual oral on a global issue across two works, and at Higher Level a 1,200 to 1,500 word essay. All of it is assessed in Modern Standard Arabic.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the practical variable is provision rather than syllabus. Some schools run Arabic A at both levels with full teaching; some run Standard Level only; some offer nothing and register self-taught candidates. Ask the IB coordinator which course and which levels are actually taught before assuming a choice exists, because it frequently does not and the self-taught route has its own limits.

programmes.name: School-supported self-taught
programmes.description: A route for a student whose Language A is not taught by the school. It applies to Literature at Standard Level and not to Higher Level or to Language and Literature. The school registers the candidate and provides a supervisor and administrative support; the teaching of the course is not part of the arrangement, which is why these candidates need an external specialist more than any other group.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has an unusually high number of students in this position, because many schools serve highly international intakes and cannot staff every Language A. A self-taught Arabic A candidate here is often the only one in their year group, with no class to discuss works with and no scheduled lesson. The plan that works is a fixed weekly session, a written reading timetable and an early decision about which works go to which component.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language and Literature in Arabic builds the analytical criteria the Diploma extends, and a student who studied Arabic at first-language level through MYP arrives with the register and the reading speed already in place. Students who took Arabic as language acquisition in MYP and then move to Arabic A face a genuine jump in both.
programmes.countryNote: The split matters more in Dubai than almost anywhere, because KHDA requires separate provision for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language and a student's placement there is a strong predictor of whether Arabic A is realistic. Checking the MYP phase and stream a student was in is the fastest way to judge whether Arabic A at Higher Level is a sensible target.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: The list below is what Arabic A actually assesses, together with the Arabic and Islamic provision a Dubai student carries alongside it. The distinction between the two sets matters, because families often buy tutoring for one while the problem sits in the other.

subjects.name: Paper 1: guided analysis
subjects.description: Previously unseen material with a guiding question - literary passages on the Literature course, non-literary texts on Language and Literature. Standard Level answers on one, Higher Level on two, and the component carries 35% at both levels. Nothing about the text can be prepared, so the preparation is a procedure applied in Arabic.

subjects.name: Paper 2: comparative essay
subjects.description: Four general questions, one chosen, two studied works compared, with no copy of either text in the room. Worth 35% at Standard Level and 25% at Higher. For Arabic A the limiting factor is almost always precise recall of quotation in Modern Standard Arabic rather than analytical ability.

subjects.name: Individual oral
subjects.description: Ten minutes of prepared analysis on a global issue across two works, followed by five minutes of questions, conducted in Arabic. Worth 30% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher. Both works are then unavailable for any other component, which makes the choice strategic.

subjects.name: HL essay
subjects.description: A 1,200 to 1,500 word essay in Arabic on one work studied, developed from the learner portfolio and worth 20% of the Higher Level grade. Not available to self-taught candidates, since the self-taught route is Standard Level only.

subjects.name: Modern Standard Arabic register
subjects.description: The assessment is written and spoken in fusha. A student fluent in Gulf, Levantine or Egyptian dialect may be entirely confident in conversation and still lose marks on written register, verb forms and vocabulary that belong to speech rather than to formal writing.

subjects.name: Works in translation
subjects.description: A Language A course requires works originally written in other languages, read in Arabic translation. Students analyse these differently from works written in Arabic: structure, imagery and context survive translation, while fine lexical choice and sound patterning belong to the translator.

subjects.name: The learner portfolio
subjects.description: Compulsory and not directly assessed. It is the source for the individual oral's global issue and, at Higher Level, the HL essay's line of inquiry. For a self-taught candidate with no class discussion, the portfolio is often the only written record of their own thinking.

subjects.name: KHDA mandatory Arabic as a first language
subjects.levels: School requirement, not an IB course
subjects.description: Mandatory in Dubai private schools whatever curriculum the school is licensed by KHDA to teach, taught in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, with Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Arabs. It is a different subject from Arabic A with different content.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.levels: School requirement, not an IB course
subjects.description: Also mandatory in Dubai private schools, with separate classes by group and language-of-instruction rules set by KHDA. Teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic are required to hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach these subjects, which is a credential a parent can reasonably ask about.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in Arabic
subjects.description: Permitted in a Group 1 language within the category rules the school will explain, and written in Arabic. A tutor may discuss a research question, suggest reading and give written feedback on the student's own drafts; the essay remains the student's work and the school supervisor stays the examining relationship.

sections.heading: What an IB DP Arabic A online tutor in Dubai is actually being asked for
paragraphs: The useful first question is not about Arabic. It is about the arrangement the student is in, because the same subject produces three entirely different pieces of work. A student in a taught class needs a second reader and marked essays. A self-taught Standard Level candidate needs the course delivered. A student weighing Arabic A against Arabic B needs a placement judgement made from written evidence rather than from how they sound at the dinner table.

Getting this wrong is expensive. Families sometimes buy a term of general Arabic conversation for a student who is already fluent and whose problem is written register in Modern Standard Arabic. Others buy literary discussion for a self-taught candidate who has not yet obtained two of the nine works and has no reading timetable. In both cases the tutoring is competent and aimed at the wrong thing, and nobody discovers it until a mock.

So the first session asks for documents. Which Arabic A course and level is the student registered for, or intending to register for. Whether the school teaches it or is supporting a self-taught candidate. The list of works. The most recent marked written piece in Arabic. And, separately, how the student is doing in the school's mandatory Arabic lessons, because those two subjects are frequently confused and the answer tells us a great deal about register.

The table-free answer to all this is short: the route determines the plan, and the route is a matter of fact rather than of preference. The sections below set out what each route actually involves, starting with the one families are given least information about.

sections.heading: The three routes into Arabic A in a Dubai school
paragraphs: Provision varies sharply across the emirate. Some Dubai schools teach Arabic A at both levels and both courses with full staffing. Some teach Standard Level Literature only. Some offer no Arabic A and will register a school-supported self-taught candidate instead. A family's realistic options are set by which of those their school is, and the answer comes from the IB coordinator rather than from the prospectus.

The self-taught route carries two hard limits that are worth repeating because they are frequently misunderstood. It applies to Language A: Literature, not to Language and Literature. And it is available at Standard Level only. A student who wants Arabic A at Higher Level needs a school that teaches it. A family planning on self-taught Higher Level is planning on something that does not exist, and discovering that after subject registration closes is a serious problem.

What the school does provide for a self-taught candidate is registration, a supervisor and the administrative handling of submissions. What it does not provide is teaching. The supervisor is not a subject teacher in this arrangement and should not be expected to mark essays weekly or teach nine works. Being clear about that boundary early keeps the relationship with the school good, which matters because every deadline and submission still goes through them.

The table below sets the three routes side by side, with what each one leaves to the family. Confirm the detail with your child's coordinator, since registration rules and school provision both change, and we publish no IB examination or results dates on this page because the IB's own site does not serve its calendar to automated checks.

sections.heading: The bilingual diploma arithmetic, including the route nobody mentions
paragraphs: A large share of Dubai families considering Arabic A are really asking about the bilingual diploma. The main route is straightforward: complete two languages from Group 1 and achieve grade 3 or above in both, and the diploma is awarded as bilingual. For an Arabic-speaking student in an English-medium Dubai school, that usually means English A plus Arabic A, which is a heavy Group 1 load but an entirely normal one.

The second route is much less discussed and sometimes more practical. A candidate who completes a subject from Group 3 or Group 4 in a language other than their nominated Language A, with grade 3 or above in both that subject and the Language A, also receives a bilingual diploma. For a student whose school teaches a humanities or science subject in Arabic, that can deliver the same outcome without carrying two full Group 1 courses.

Both routes depend on grades rather than on registration alone, which is worth saying plainly. A student who registers for Arabic A and finishes with a 2 does not get a bilingual diploma and has spent two years on a seventh commitment. The honest question in Year 11 is therefore not whether the student would like a bilingual diploma but whether a 3 or better in Arabic A is a realistic target given their written fusha, and a marked piece of writing answers that better than a conversation.

Nothing about this requires tutoring, and no honest page should imply it does. What tutoring can do is give you the evidence for the decision before subject choices close, and then support whichever route the family picks.

sections.heading: Fusha, dialect and the register problem in a Dubai household
paragraphs: Arabic A is assessed in Modern Standard Arabic. Most students in Dubai speak a dialect at home - Gulf, Levantine, Egyptian, Iraqi, Sudanese, Maghrebi - and move between dialect and fusha without thinking about it. That bilingual facility is an asset in conversation and a liability in an examination script, because the dialect forms are invisible to the student. They do not feel like errors; they feel like Arabic.

The errors are predictable enough to drill. Verb conjugation patterns that have levelled in speech, case endings dropped in the spoken form, vocabulary that is ordinary in dialect and wrong in formal writing, and sentence structures that work aloud and read as speech on paper. A student who logs their own corrected errors for a month usually finds the same six or seven patterns repeating, and once they are named they stop appearing within a term.

This is also why fluency is a bad placement signal. A student who converses confidently in Arabic may write at a level that will not sustain Arabic A, and a quieter student who reads Arabic literature comfortably may be a strong candidate. The test that answers the question is a piece of timed written analysis in fusha, marked honestly. It takes one session and it prevents a two-year mistake.

A note on the mandatory Arabic lessons here, because the two subjects interact. KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Arabic as a first language, which means a student in that stream is already working in fusha for part of the week. A student in the non-Arab stream is not, and that difference shows up quickly in Arabic A written work. Knowing which stream a student has been in is one of the more useful pieces of background a tutor can have.

sections.heading: Choosing and obtaining works in Arabic
paragraphs: For a taught course the school chooses the works. For a self-taught Standard Level candidate the choice is made with the supervisor, and it is where a good decision saves a year of difficulty. Nine works at Standard Level, drawn with the required balance of works originally written in Arabic, works in translation, and a limited allowance of freely chosen titles, covering several literary forms, periods and regions.

Two practical filters are worth applying before any literary judgement. The first is obtainability in Dubai, in the edition the student will cite from: page references matter for close reading, and a student working from a different printing than their supervisor creates a steady low-level problem for two years. The older bookshops in Bur Dubai and Al Karama remain the best physical source for Arabic titles in the city. The second filter is length. A poetry collection and a long modern novel both count as one work and demand completely different amounts of evening reading.

Then the allocation rule applies, exactly as it does in every Language A: a work used for one assessment component cannot be used for another. The individual oral needs two works, one of which must be a work in translation and the other originally written in Arabic. Paper 2 needs two more. For a self-taught Standard Level candidate that is four of nine committed, and the decision should be taken in the autumn of Year 12 rather than discovered in the spring of Year 13.

On works in translation specifically, Arabic A students make the same mistake English A students make in reverse: they analyse the Arabic of a translated novel as though the author had chosen those words. Structure, narrative method, imagery and context all survive translation and are fully available for analysis. The translator's diction is not. Two short written exercises settle this permanently.

sections.heading: Arabic A and the KHDA mandatory subjects are two different things
paragraphs: This is the single most common confusion in Dubai, and it is worth separating completely. Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, under requirements KHDA has set out and which schools were required to implement by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. Arabic A is an IB Diploma subject the student chose. They share a language and nothing else.

The KHDA requirements are specific in ways that affect a student's week. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, and for Social Studies for Arab students, while non-Arabs are taught Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language.

Instructional time is counted in 40-minute lesson units. Schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes. For the mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, which is a real constraint on what any tutoring material for those lessons can look like - and a reason to be sceptical of anyone selling a bespoke curriculum for them.

One further credential point a parent can reasonably check: schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. That applies to the school's staff. It is not something IB Gram holds or could hold, and any tutoring service implying otherwise about itself is misrepresenting a specific regulatory permission.

sections.heading: Where Arabic sits in Ministry of Education equivalency
paragraphs: Families frequently assume that strong Arabic helps with the Ministry of Education equivalency a UAE university application depends on. For the British track the published position is the opposite of that assumption. A student must show five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade no lower than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

For the American track the published requirements are about English and mathematics rather than Arabic: English proficiency evidenced by a score of 5 in IELTS academic, 61 in TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and at least 450 in SAT Mathematics before applying. One ranking competitor states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the published rule is five, and getting that detail right matters more than anything else on this subject.

For the International Baccalaureate we will not publish a points threshold. We have not read one on the Ministry's own site, and an unsourced figure on a page like this would be repeated by families as fact. Ask the Ministry of Education or your emirate's attestation authority directly for the IB position, and treat any site that quotes a specific IB equivalency score without citing the Ministry with caution.

Two further points. Equivalency and attestation are processes the authorities run, not services IB Gram performs or guarantees, and nothing about tutoring is required for either. The sensible use of this information is planning: a student choosing subjects in Year 11 should know which of them will count towards equivalency, because Arabic A may be the right choice for a bilingual diploma while counting for nothing in that particular arithmetic.

sections.heading: Why Arabic A tuition for Dubai is delivered online, and what the market charges
paragraphs: Dubai families often begin by looking for an Arabic tutor who will come to the house, which is the traditional pattern here, so both halves of this deserve a straight answer. IB Gram delivers tuition to UAE families as one-to-one lessons over live video on Gulf Standard Time. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and no line on this site should be read as an offer of one in Dubai.

For Arabic A the supply argument is stronger than for almost any other subject. Plenty of people in Dubai can teach Arabic. The number who have taught the IB Diploma's Arabic A course, who know what criterion B asks for in a Paper 1 on an unseen Arabic passage, and who can mark an essay in fusha against the published descriptors is far smaller. The chance that one of them lives within a short drive of a given community is low, and restricting the search to that radius means selecting an Arabic teacher instead of an Arabic A teacher.

The format also fits the work. Essays are annotated on a shared screen in Arabic and saved, so a register error log accumulates across a term instead of living on loose paper. Oral rehearsals are recorded without arranging anything, which is how a student hears their own register sliding into dialect. And a self-taught Standard Level candidate - who by definition has no class - gets a scheduled weekly teaching session that does not depend on anybody's commute.

They are market rates and not an IB Gram price list; the route in here is a free trial lesson and a consultation, because the rate depends on the route, the level and availability. sections.heading: Academic honesty, permits and what we will not do
paragraphs: The individual oral, the HL essay and the Extended Essay must be the student's own work, and on a self-taught course the temptation to blur that is higher than anywhere else, because there is no class and no teacher checking progress weekly. So the boundary is stated before the first session. A tutor teaches the works, explains what each criterion asks for, questions a line of inquiry until the student sharpens it, and gives written feedback on drafts the student has produced. Nobody supplies prose in Arabic, nobody rewrites paragraphs, and nobody provides an argument to be adopted.

We also do not distribute IB, Cambridge or Pearson documents. Subject guides, prescribed reading lists, past material and mark schemes belong to the boards, and a tutor cites the official page while the school or family obtains them properly. For the KHDA mandatory subjects there is an additional and specific rule: using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, so any service offering its own curriculum for those lessons is offering something the school cannot use.

On permits, the UAE position is clear and parents should ask about it directly. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time on its own service page. Individuals tutoring without the permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no fine schedule has been published, nobody should quote you an amount.

One more boundary that applies with particular force to Arabic. Abu Dhabi's ADEK professional-ethics rules prohibit private and charter school staff from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Asking your child's own Arabic teacher for paid lessons is therefore the wrong route, however convenient it looks.

process.title: Establish the route first
process.description: Which Arabic A course and level the student is registered for, whether the school teaches it or is supporting a self-taught candidate, and the list of works. That single question decides whether the job is marking essays or delivering a course, and the two plans share almost nothing.

process.title: Send a marked piece of written Arabic
process.description: A timed analytical piece in fusha, marked if possible. It answers the placement question, shows which register errors are recurring, and tells a tutor whether the student's difficulty is analysis, recall or written Arabic itself. Conversation cannot show any of that.

process.title: See two named Arabic A tutors
process.description: Names, which Arabic A course and level each has taught, whether they support self-taught candidates, and Gulf Standard Time availability. Teaching Arabic and teaching Arabic A are different jobs, and we say which one a tutor has done.

process.title: Fix the works and the allocation
process.description: For a self-taught candidate, a dated reading timetable across both years and the allocation of works to the oral and Paper 2 decided in Year 12. For a taught candidate, the same allocation check against the school's plan, because no work may be used for two components.

process.title: Review at week eight
process.description: Per-criterion scores on marked written work, the register error log, and the reading timetable checked against reality. We go through it with you and decide whether to continue, change the balance, change tutor, or stop.

whyPoints.title: Arabic A, not Arabic in general
whyPoints.description: The scarce thing is not a tutor who speaks Arabic but one who has taught the Diploma course and can mark an essay in fusha against the published criteria. We say which of the two a tutor is before you book, because a term of general Arabic conversation helps a fluent student very little.

whyPoints.title: Self-taught candidates treated as a real route
whyPoints.description: Literature at Standard Level may be taken school-supported self-taught, and those candidates get no teaching from the school. We plan for that explicitly - a dated reading timetable, weekly teaching, early component allocation - rather than offering feedback on work nobody has taught them to produce.

whyPoints.title: Register errors named and logged
whyPoints.description: Dialect forms are invisible to the student who uses them. We log corrected errors across a term, and the six or seven recurring patterns usually stop appearing once they have been named. That is faster than any amount of general grammar revision.

IB Gram holds no approval from any of these bodies.

faqs.question: What is school-supported self-taught Arabic A and who can take it?
faqs.answer: It is the route for a student whose Language A is not taught by their school. The school registers the candidate, assigns a supervisor and handles submissions; it does not teach the course. Two limits matter and are frequently missed: the route applies to Language A: Literature rather than Language and Literature, and it is available at Standard Level only. In practice a self-taught candidate carries nine works, an individual oral and two papers with no class and no scheduled lesson, which is why these students need an external specialist more than any other group.

faqs.question: Can my child sit Arabic A at Higher Level if the school does not teach it?
faqs.answer: No. The school-supported self-taught route is Standard Level only, and it covers Literature rather than Language and Literature. A student who needs Arabic A at Higher Level needs a school that actually teaches it, which in Dubai means asking the IB coordinator directly rather than relying on a prospectus. This is worth settling before subject registration closes, because a family planning on self-taught Higher Level is planning on something that does not exist, and the discovery afterwards is a genuine problem rather than a paperwork one.

faqs.question: Can a student get the bilingual diploma without taking two Group 1 languages?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this route is rarely mentioned. A candidate who completes a subject from Group 3 or Group 4 in a language other than their nominated Language A, with grade 3 or above in both that subject and the Language A, receives a bilingual diploma. Whether it is available depends entirely on whether your child's school teaches a humanities or science subject in Arabic, which is less common in Dubai's international schools but worth asking about. The main route remains two Group 1 languages at grade 3 or above.

faqs.question: Which Arabic A course do Dubai schools usually offer, and can we request the other?
faqs.answer: Provision varies more than families expect. Some Dubai schools teach both Arabic A courses at both levels, some run Standard Level Literature only, and some offer none and register self-taught candidates. Requesting a course the school does not staff rarely succeeds, because it needs a teacher and a viable class. The practical sequence is to ask the coordinator what is actually taught this year, then decide between that, Arabic B, and the self-taught Standard Level Literature route if one is needed.

faqs.question: Does the mandatory Arabic lesson at my child's Dubai school count towards Arabic A?
faqs.answer: No. They are separate subjects that happen to share a language. Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools whatever curriculum the school is licensed by KHDA to teach, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students and combined classes prohibited. Arabic A is a Diploma subject with its own works, criteria and assessments. A student can be doing well in one and poorly in the other, and the mandatory lessons are often the better predictor of written register in fusha.

faqs.question: My child speaks Gulf dialect at home. How much does that help with Arabic A?
faqs.answer: It helps with confidence and comprehension and very little with written marks, because the assessment is in Modern Standard Arabic. Dialect forms are invisible to the student who uses them - they feel like Arabic, not like errors - so they appear in essays unnoticed. The recurring problems are levelled verb patterns, dropped case endings, vocabulary that is ordinary in speech and wrong in formal writing, and sentence shapes that read as speech on paper. Logged over a month, those usually reduce to six or seven patterns that stop appearing once named.

faqs.question: Where can we obtain the Arabic set works in the edition the school uses?
faqs.answer: Edition matters more than families expect, because page references are used in class discussion and in close reading, and a student working from a different printing has a low-level problem for two years. The older bookshops in Bur Dubai and Al Karama remain the best physical source for Arabic titles in the city, and the school's Arabic department can usually tell you which printing it uses. For a self-taught candidate this is worth sorting in the first fortnight of Year 12 rather than discovering mid-course.

faqs.question: How does Paper 2 work in Arabic when no copy of the texts is allowed?
faqs.answer: Four general questions are given, the student chooses one and compares two of the works studied, with no text in the room. For Arabic A the binding constraint is almost always precise recall of quotation in fusha rather than analytical ability. The remedy is a bank of around fifteen precisely remembered moments per work, chosen because they serve several possible questions rather than one, and tested aloud each session. A student who understood both works but cannot quote them accurately writes a vague essay.

faqs.question: Does Arabic count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: For the British track, no. The Ministry requires five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade no lower than E or 3, plus one A-Level at no lower than E or two AS-Levels at the same grade, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five required subjects. The American track requirements concern English and mathematics scores. For the IB we will not restate a points threshold, because we have not read one on the Ministry's own site; verify it with the Ministry or your emirate's attestation authority directly.

faqs.question: Are non-Arab students able to take Arabic A?
faqs.answer: Group 1 placement is about working at first-language level in the language, not about nationality, so a non-Arab student with genuinely first-language Arabic can be placed in Arabic A. In practice it is uncommon, because the reading load in fusha is substantial and most non-Arab students in Dubai are better served by Arabic B in Group 2. The test is a timed piece of written analysis in Modern Standard Arabic, marked honestly. It takes one session and it is far more reliable than judging from conversation.

faqs.question: What does an online Arabic A tutor in Dubai charge per hour?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai market rates in October 2026 run roughly AED 45-150 for budget online tutors, AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180-500 for in-home visits with travel, and AED 200-450 or more for an IB specialist, with one premium provider publishing AED 650. Those belong to the providers who published them and are quoted with that attribution rather than as our own prices. For Arabic A the relevant band is the specialist one, because the scarce qualification is having taught the Diploma course rather than having taught Arabic.

faqs.question: Is in-home Arabic tutoring available anywhere in the UAE through IB Gram?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Dubai families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For Arabic A the trade is clearly worth making, because the pool of tutors who have actually taught the Diploma's Arabic A course is small, and choosing from people who can reach your community by five o'clock usually means choosing an Arabic teacher rather than an Arabic A teacher.

faqs.question: Can an Arabic A tutor also help with Islamic Education?
faqs.answer: Better handled as a separate question, and with a caution. For the KHDA mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, so a tutor cannot supply a bespoke curriculum for those lessons. Schools are also required to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach them, which applies to school staff rather than to a private tutor. Support there is realistically limited to study skills and the school's own material.

faqs.question: How do Ramadan and the Dubai exam season change an Arabic A plan?
faqs.answer: Both need to be in the plan from the start rather than handled as interruptions. During Ramadan the household day shifts and many families prefer post-Iftar sessions, which is simple to arrange when nobody is travelling. Long works are far easier to finish in a holiday block than in a Year 13 term, so a reading timetable should deliberately place the longest work in a break. Internal submission deadlines do not move for either, which is the argument for front-loading reading into Year 12 while the pressure is lower.

faqs.question: My child is a heritage speaker who reads Arabic slowly. Is Arabic A realistic?
faqs.answer: It depends on reading speed in fusha rather than on speaking, and it is measurable. A student who speaks fluently but reads formal Arabic at half the pace of a classmate will struggle with nine works and with a timed unseen paper, and the honest answer may be Arabic B. The way to decide is a timed reading comprehension and a timed written analysis in Modern Standard Arabic, taken before subject choices close. Making that decision from evidence in Year 11 is far better than discovering it in a Year 13 mock.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-online-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB DP Arabic A online tutor in Dubai, the first thing to settle is which arrangement your child is in: a taught Arabic A class, a school-supported self-taught Standard Level registration, or a placement decision still to be made between Arabic A and Arabic B. Send the works list if there is one, plus a timed piece of written analysis in Modern Standard Arabic. From those we can tell you what is realistic, what the bilingual diploma would require, and what the first six weeks should contain. The trial lesson is free and sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed below teach IB Arabic A at HL and SL, in both the Literature and the Language and Literature routes. Each profile names the components they have taught most, whether they work in the Literature or the Language and Literature course, and the hours they hold in Gulf Standard Time.

intro.heading: Fluent at home, marked in Modern Standard Arabic
paragraphs: Arabic A is a Group 1 course: studies in language and literature, taken by students whose strongest language is Arabic. In Dubai it is the course that lets a first-language Arabic speaker take English B in Group 2, and it is the course most often underestimated by the families of students who speak Arabic every day. Speaking Arabic and writing graded literary analysis in Modern Standard Arabic are separate skills, and the Diploma assesses only the second.

The structural reason is diglossia. A student raised in Dubai speaks Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine or Maghrebi dialect at home and with friends, hears Modern Standard Arabic in formal media and in school, and is examined entirely in Modern Standard Arabic. Dialect vocabulary and dialect syntax leak into written responses under time pressure. Case endings, verb conjugation in the formal register and the vocabulary of literary criticism are the three places examiners see it most. None of that reflects a weak Arabic speaker; it reflects a student who has never been made to write formally for an hour at a stretch.

The second problem is critical vocabulary. Arabic A asks for analysis of how a text produces meaning, which requires a working lexicon of literary and rhetorical terms in Arabic. Students who studied Arabic as a school subject rather than as an analytical discipline arrive in Year 12 able to summarise a poem and unable to discuss its structure, voice, imagery or the effect of a particular construction. Summary earns very little under the Arabic A criteria. Analysis earns almost all of it.

The third is reading volume. Arabic A requires studied works across periods, places and forms, and the works are read in Arabic. A student who reads fluently in English and slowly in Arabic will finish Year 12 without having properly read the set works, which makes the Paper 2 comparative essay and the individual oral guesswork. This is the single most predictable Arabic A failure in Dubai and the one most easily prevented by a reading schedule set in September rather than in April.

There is a fourth issue that is administrative rather than linguistic. Arabic A classes in Dubai Diploma cohorts are small, often four or five students taught by one specialist who covers HL and SL in the same room. That teacher knows every student well and has no second group to calibrate against, no co-marker for the HL essay drafts, and no spare period to re-teach a timed paper that went badly. Parents read the small class size as individual attention. In practice it means the student's only reader is also their assessor, which is the specific gap one-to-one work closes.

Lessons are one-to-one over live video, in Arabic, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time so a session can begin after a Dubai school day ends. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE - sending a tutor to an address is a service we run only in India - which means your child is matched to a tutor who teaches the Arabic A criteria rather than to whichever Arabic teacher is available within a short drive of your community.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic A sits in the Diploma, but a Dubai student's readiness for it is decided much earlier, in the Arabic stream their school placed them in at primary level. These are the IB programmes around it and what each actually contributes to a student's formal Arabic.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, one per group, three at Higher Level. Arabic A occupies Group 1 for a first-language Arabic speaker, freeing Group 2 for English B or French B. The course assesses guided analysis of unseen text, comparative essay writing on studied works, an individual oral on a global issue, and at HL a separate essay. All of it is produced in Modern Standard Arabic.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai, Arabic A classes are frequently small - sometimes four or five students in a Diploma cohort of a hundred - which means the class moves at the pace of the strongest reader and the teacher has no second set to compare against. A small class is not the same as individual attention, and it is one of the clearer reasons Dubai families seek Arabic A support.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Language and literature in the MYP is assessed across four criteria: analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. A student in the Arabic language-and-literature stream rather than the acquisition stream is on the path to Arabic A. The MYP rewards analysis earlier than most national curricula do, so students who completed it are usually better prepared for Arabic A Paper 1 than students who came through an Arabic-as-a-subject route.
programmes.countryNote: The practical Dubai problem is stream placement. Many schools place students into the Arabic first-language stream by nationality or home language rather than by assessed reading level, which puts weaker readers into the harder stream and vice versa. A student can sit in the first-language MYP stream for five years without ever having read a full literary work in Arabic unaided.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The Primary Years Programme embeds language learning in transdisciplinary units. For Arabic in a Dubai PYP school the question is whether the child is in the Arabic-for-Arabs stream, where Standard Arabic is the language of instruction, or the additional-language stream. The stream decided at primary level is the one that largely determines whether Arabic A is realistic at sixteen.
programmes.countryNote: KHDA guidance requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. For parents that is a checkable point: ask which stream your child is in and what the weekly instructional time is.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-tutor.subjectsIntro: Arabic A rarely travels alone. A Dubai Diploma student taking it is usually also taking English B, sometimes Islamic Education at school level, and often needs help with the core. These are the courses IB Gram covers around it.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Non-literary and literary texts together. Paper 1 is guided analysis of unseen non-literary material in Arabic - advertising, journalism, speeches. Paper 2 compares studied literary works. The most commonly chosen Arabic A route in Dubai because the non-literary half feels closer to what students already read.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Literature
subjects.description: Literary works only, across periods, places and forms, read in Arabic. Paper 1 is guided literary analysis of an unseen extract. Demanding on reading volume and on the critical lexicon, and chosen mainly by students heading for Arabic literature, law or journalism.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The Group 2 acquisition route for students with conversational Arabic and limited Modern Standard Arabic. A common destination for students moved out of Arabic A in Year 12, which is a decision worth taking deliberately rather than by drift.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: For genuine beginners with no prior Arabic. Not available to a student who has studied Arabic at school, which rules it out for most Dubai residents. Useful to know about when a family is weighing what their child is actually eligible for.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: The Group 2 pairing most Arabic A students in Dubai take. Paper 1 productive writing in a named text type, Paper 2 listening and reading, and an individual oral. Timetabling the two language courses together is the planning question families most often get wrong.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Taken alongside Arabic A by students pursuing a bilingual diploma through two Group 1 languages. A heavy combination: two sets of studied works, two individual orals and, at HL, two separate essays in the same academic year.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word essay on a prescribed title plus the exhibition. Students who think in Arabic and write TOK in English often lose marks on precision of argument rather than on ideas, which is a specific and fixable problem.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in Arabic A
subjects.description: A 4,000-word essay written in Arabic on a studied or self-chosen literary question. Supervision covers research question scope, source quality and structure. The writing remains the student's own work throughout, as the IB requires.

subjects.name: IGCSE Arabic as a First Language
subjects.description: The qualification many Dubai students hold before the Diploma. It rewards comprehension and directed writing rather than literary analysis, which is precisely the gap Arabic A Paper 1 exposes in the first term of Year 12.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-tutor.regionsIntro: Requests for Arabic A support in Dubai come disproportionately from the communities with large Arab resident populations and from the schools that run genuine first-language Arabic streams. The notes below are about what each area's school mix means for session planning.

regions.name: Al Mizhar and Al Khawaneej
regions.note: Large Emirati and Arab expatriate households with children in English-medium IB schools. Arabic A demand here is high and usually paired with English B. Sessions commonly run after 17:00 because families eat later and the school run is long.

regions.name: Nad Al Sheba and Meydan
regions.note: Newer communities with recently opened IB schools and small Diploma cohorts, which means very small Arabic A classes. Parents here frequently ask for a second reader for the studied works because the class has no comparison group.

regions.name: Al Qusais and Al Twar
regions.note: Established schools with long-standing Arabic departments. Students often have strong Quranic and classical Arabic exposure and weak critical vocabulary, which is an unusual profile: the reading is secure and the analysis language is missing.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim and Jumeirah 3
regions.note: A mix of Emirati and mixed-nationality households where Arabic is one of two or three home languages. Arabic A here often competes for study time with sport and music commitments, so fortnightly longer sessions fit better than weekly short ones.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Fast-growing Diploma cohorts in schools that opened within the last decade. Arabic A is frequently taught by a single teacher covering SL and HL together, which makes external HL essay support the most requested item in this area.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Circle and Al Furjan
regions.note: High proportion of mid-year school transfers, so students join Arabic A with a different set of studied works behind them. The first sessions are usually spent reconciling two reading lists rather than teaching anything new.

regions.name: Ras Al Khor and Dubai Festival City
regions.note: Schools with Arabic-medium roots now running the Diploma alongside other routes. Students here are often the strongest formal writers in the city and the least practised at timed unseen analysis, which is a Paper 1 problem specifically.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai schools with large Arabic first-language Diploma cohorts
schoolClusters.note: In these schools the Arabic A class is big enough to be streamed and the department carries more than one specialist. Students arriving from them generally have the reading volume and need work on the critical register and on timed Paper 1 technique.

schoolClusters.city: IB continuum schools running Arabic A from the Middle Years Programme
schoolClusters.note: Continuum schools carry students through PYP, MYP and the Diploma, so the Arabic stream a child entered at five is usually the one they sit at eighteen. Students from these schools tend to analyse confidently and read less widely than their teachers assume.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-a-tutor.modesIntro: Arabic A support in Dubai divides neatly by what is actually missing: the formal register, a reading schedule, or one assessed component that is close. Each of the three is delivered one-to-one in Arabic over live video.

modes.title: Modern Standard Arabic register rebuild
modes.description: For the student whose spoken Arabic is fluent and whose written Arabic carries dialect. Weekly timed writing in Modern Standard Arabic, returned marked for register, case endings and critical vocabulary rather than for content. Usually eight to twelve weeks, and best started in Year 12 rather than in the term before the papers.

modes.title: Studied works reading programme
modes.description: A reading schedule across the set works, with discussion sessions at fixed points rather than at the end. The tutor works through the passages most likely to supply an oral extract or a Paper 2 comparison, and the student builds quotation and context notes as they go. This is the intervention that prevents the Year 13 panic rather than managing it.

modes.title: Single-component work: HL essay or individual oral
modes.description: Four to eight sessions on one assessed piece. For the HL essay that means narrowing a line of inquiry to something arguable in 1,200 to 1,500 words and reviewing the student's own drafts against the four criteria. For the oral it means global-issue selection, extract work across two texts, and rehearsal with playback.

sections.heading: Why first-language Arabic speakers lose marks in Arabic A
paragraphs: The assumption behind most Arabic A disappointments in Dubai is that a student who speaks Arabic at home starts the course with an advantage. In conversation they do. In the examination they do not, because every component is produced in Modern Standard Arabic and marked for analytical precision in that register. A student can hold a complex argument aloud in Gulf dialect and lose marks for case endings and verb forms when the same argument is written down.

The failures group into four kinds, and each has a different remedy. Register failures are mechanical and respond quickly to timed writing with marked feedback. Critical-vocabulary failures need a lexicon built deliberately over weeks, because the words for structure, voice, register, irony and effect are not the words a student uses at home. Reading-volume failures cannot be fixed late; they need a schedule. Analysis failures - summarising rather than arguing - are the deepest, and they take a term of being asked the right question until the habit changes.

A diagnostic session distinguishes these in about forty minutes. Give the student an unseen text in Arabic, forty minutes, and the Paper 1 instruction, and the script tells a specialist which of the four problems they have. That is why the trial lesson in Arabic A is a writing session rather than a conversation. A conversation in Arabic with a fluent Dubai teenager tells you almost nothing about the grade they will get.
bullets: Register: dialect interference under time pressure, fixable in weeks
Critical lexicon: the vocabulary of analysis, built over a term
Reading volume: fixable only with a schedule set early
Summary instead of argument: the deepest problem and the slowest to shift

sections.heading: Arabic A: Literature or Arabic A: Language and Literature?
paragraphs: Two Group 1 routes exist in Arabic and Dubai schools do not always offer both. Literature studies literary works only. Language and Literature adds non-literary texts - journalism, advertising, speeches, political writing - and makes them the material for Paper 1. The choice changes what Paper 1 looks like, how much reading the course demands, and which students find it manageable.

In practice Language and Literature suits the larger share of Dubai students, because the non-literary half uses material they already encounter and because the analytical moves transfer from what they do in English. Literature suits the student who reads Arabic poetry and prose for pleasure and wants a degree in the field. The route is usually chosen by the school rather than the family, based on which specialist the department has, so the useful parental question is which route your child is on rather than which one they would prefer.

Where the choice is genuinely open, the deciding factor should be reading speed in Arabic rather than enthusiasm. A student who reads Arabic prose at half their English pace will not complete the Literature reading list in two years alongside five other subjects, however much they enjoy it. Measure it before deciding: time the student on ten pages of unfamiliar Arabic prose and ten pages of English, and compare. A ratio worse than two to one makes the Literature route a workload decision rather than a preference.

One further practical point applies in Dubai specifically. Mid-year transfers between schools are common, and the two routes do not transfer cleanly: a student moving from a Language and Literature class into a Literature class arrives with non-literary study behind them that no longer counts and literary works they have not read. Where a move is coming, ask both schools which route and which studied works they run before the transfer rather than after, because the reconciliation work falls on the student either way. The table sets out what each route asks for so the conversation with the Diploma coordinator can be specific.

sections.heading: The assessed components and what each is worth
paragraphs: Arabic A has three components at SL and four at HL. Paper 1 is guided analysis of an unseen text, under timed conditions, with a guiding question. Paper 2 is a comparative essay on studied works, written from memory without the texts in front of the student. The individual oral examines a global issue through two studied works and is marked out of forty across four criteria. At HL a separate essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on one studied work is added, and the Paper 2 weighting shifts to accommodate it.

The component most Dubai students underrate is Paper 2. It is written without the texts, so it depends entirely on what the student can recall: quotations, context, structural features, and a comparison that was planned before the exam rather than invented in it. Students who have read the works but never built comparison grids write two separate summaries joined by the word 'however' and score in the middle bands regardless of how well they know the books.

Every weighting and word limit named here should be confirmed against the current Arabic A subject guide held by your child's Diploma coordinator before you build a revision plan around it, because the IB revises course structures on a cycle and schools set internal deadlines well ahead of the external ones. The value of the table below is the shape of the course and where marks go, which does not move year to year.

sections.heading: The individual oral: one global issue, two works, forty marks
paragraphs: The Arabic A individual oral asks the student to examine how a global issue is presented in two works - one literary and one non-literary in Language and Literature, two literary in Literature. The student prepares, delivers a sustained oral, and then answers the teacher's questions. It is marked out of forty across four criteria: knowledge, understanding and interpretation; analysis and evaluation; focus and organisation; and language. The recording goes to the IB for moderation.

Two failures dominate in Dubai. The first is a global issue chosen too wide. 'Identity' is not a global issue; 'the loss of dialect identity in Gulf urban migration as presented in these two extracts' is. A wide issue produces an oral that floats above both texts and scores poorly on analysis and evaluation however fluent the Arabic. The second is extract choice: students pick passages they like rather than passages dense enough to analyse for ten minutes, then run out of material at minute six.

Both are preparation problems, which is good news, because preparation is the part a tutor can rehearse. Narrowing the issue takes one session. Choosing and annotating two extracts takes two. After that it is repetition: deliver, record, play back, answer the questions a moderator would ask about the link between the issue and the extract. Students who have rehearsed this five times speak with the pacing that the language criterion rewards, and they stop reciting.

The question phase is where Dubai students most often undersell themselves. After the prepared oral the teacher asks questions, and a student who has memorised a script has nothing left once the script runs out. Answers shrink to a sentence, and the organisation and language marks fall with them. The remedy is to prepare an argument rather than a text: five claims the student can defend, each tied to a specific line in one of the extracts, so that any question lands somewhere they have evidence. Rehearsal with an adult who asks awkward questions in Arabic is the only way to build that, and it is not something a student can do alone.
bullets: Four criteria, ten marks each, forty in total
A global issue narrow enough to argue, not a theme
Extracts chosen for analytical density, not for preference
Recorded and moderated, so a weak attempt cannot be quietly repeated

sections.heading: The HL essay: 1,200 to 1,500 words that are the student's own
paragraphs: The HL essay is a formal written exploration of one studied work, in a line of inquiry the student chooses, inside a tight word range. It is the Arabic A component where Dubai students most often need outside help and the one where the academic-honesty line matters most, because it is submitted work and it is written outside the examination hall over weeks.

The commonest problem is scope. A student picks a question like 'the theme of exile in this novel' and writes a survey. The criteria reward a narrow, arguable claim developed with textual evidence, which means a question closer to 'how the novel's shifting narrator positions the reader against the exile's own account'. Narrowing is the work, and a tutor can do it legitimately by asking questions until the student's own idea sharpens. Nobody can do it for them without compromising the submission.

What a tutor may do with an HL essay: discuss possible lines of inquiry, explain the four criteria and what each rewards, read a draft the student has written and ask questions about its argument, point out where evidence is thin, and advise on structure in general terms. What a tutor may not do: write any part of it, dictate sentences, rewrite paragraphs, or supply an outline the student fills in. The school supervisor signs the authenticity declaration, and an IB malpractice finding follows a candidate for the rest of their application cycle.

The word range is tighter than it looks, and that is a planning point rather than a style point. Fifteen hundred words in Arabic carries less content than fifteen hundred words in English, because Arabic constructions are denser and quotation eats space quickly. A student who plans four sections will write a summary of each; a student who plans two will have room to argue. The drafting order that works is to choose the extract passages first, build the claim from what the evidence actually supports, and only then write an introduction - which is the reverse of how most students approach it and the reason so many Dubai HL essays open with a paragraph the rest of the essay never earns.
bullets: 1,200-1,500 words, HL only, on one studied work
Marked across knowledge and interpretation, analysis, organisation and language
Narrow arguable claim beats broad thematic survey every time
Tutor reads and questions; the student writes every sentence

sections.heading: KHDA's mandatory Arabic rules and what they mean for your child
paragraphs: Dubai private schools are overseen by KHDA, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Alongside inspection, KHDA sets requirements for the mandatory UAE subjects that run in every Dubai private school regardless of the licensed international curriculum. For an Arabic A family these rules are directly relevant, because they govern how much formal Arabic a child has received before Year 12 and in what language it was taught.

KHDA guidance requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools, with implementation from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. Schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language.

Two further points are worth asking your school about directly. KHDA requires that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a credential you are entitled to ask about. And instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with schools permitted to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and a recommendation that no mandatory subject lesson runs shorter than 25 minutes. A school meeting the weekly minimum in short fragments delivers less usable Arabic than one running full periods.
