dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.tutorsIntro: The mentors below have run or supervised CAS programmes rather than taught a syllabus. Their work is planning, evidence mapping and reflection quality — and knowing which gaps a Dubai school's coordinator will question at the final interview.

intro.heading: The component with no marks that can still cost a Diploma
paragraphs: Creativity, Activity, Service is the third core component of the Diploma and the only one that carries no grade. There is no mark scheme, no examiner and no band descriptor. What there is instead is a completion requirement: a student must provide evidence of having achieved all seven CAS learning outcomes, maintain a portfolio, complete a CAS project lasting at least one month, and attend three documented interviews with the school's coordinator. Fail to complete it and the Diploma is not awarded, whatever the six subject grades say.

That asymmetry is why CAS behaves differently from every other part of the programme. There is no upside — nobody gets extra points for an exceptional portfolio — and the downside is total. Students respond rationally by deprioritising it, because nothing is due tomorrow and nothing is marked. Then the final interview arrives, the coordinator asks for evidence of an outcome the student never addressed, and a component that was never difficult becomes urgent in the same term as the Extended Essay and final examinations.

The second thing families in Dubai consistently get wrong is the hours. The old requirement of a set number of hours was removed years ago, and there is no hour target to hit. What replaced it is harder to manage and better pedagogically: a reasonable balance across the three strands, over at least eighteen months, evidenced against the seven outcomes. Parents still ask us how many hours are needed, and schools still occasionally quote the old figure, which is how students end up logging time instead of building evidence.

The third is the nature of the work. CAS cannot be tutored, because there is nothing to learn. What can be mentored is planning: which outcomes are already covered by things the student does anyway, which are genuinely missing, how to design a CAS project that satisfies the collaboration and duration requirements without inventing a charity, what a reflection has to contain to be worth writing, and what the coordinator will ask at each of the three interviews. Most families need two or three sessions in total, and we say so rather than selling a weekly slot.

IB Gram matches your child with a CAS mentor who works one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time around the Dubai school day. Tuition and mentoring for UAE families is delivered online. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. A free trial lesson comes first, one per family, with no card details taken. The student does every activity and writes every reflection — nobody else can, and a portfolio that was not built by the student is an academic honesty problem rather than a shortcut.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.programmesIntro: Service and self-directed activity appear throughout the IB, and how a student handled the earlier version usually predicts how CAS will go. These are the stages we work across in Dubai.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: CAS runs for a minimum of eighteen months, normally from the start of DP1 to the second half of DP2. The student records experiences and reflections in a portfolio, evidences all seven learning outcomes, carries out a CAS project of at least one month involving collaboration, and attends three documented interviews with the coordinator. There is no mark and no grade; there is a completion requirement.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools run very different CAS systems. Some use a structured online platform with monthly checkpoints; others rely on a single adviser and an end-of-term reminder. Ask which model your child's school uses and when the three interviews fall, because the answer decides whether outside mentoring is useful at all.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP includes service as action throughout the programme and culminates in the personal project, which is self-directed, supervised and recorded in a process journal. A student who kept that journal honestly already has the habit CAS depends on. A student who produced it retrospectively usually repeats the pattern with the CAS portfolio two years later.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has a large IB continuum population, so some DP1 students arrive with four years of service-as-action behind them while others, arriving from IGCSE, have never recorded a reflection. The second group needs a planning session in the first term, not a rescue in DP2.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme core includes service learning rather than CAS, alongside personal and professional skills, language development and the reflective project. Service learning follows a similar investigate-prepare-act-reflect cycle, so the planning and reflection coaching transfers almost unchanged.
programmes.countryNote: A small number of Dubai schools offer the CP. Families occasionally ask us for CAS help when the requirement on the registration is service learning, so the first thing we confirm is which programme the student is enrolled in and which document the coordinator actually wants.

programmes.name: CAS with TOK and the Extended Essay
programmes.description: Two core components carry points and one carries a veto. TOK and the Extended Essay are graded A to E and combine for up to three Diploma points; CAS is pass-or-not-complete. The practical difference is that CAS cannot be improved by extra effort in the final month, because the evidence has to have accumulated over at least eighteen months.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the CAS final interview frequently sits in the same weeks as the Extended Essay submission and subject internal assessment deadlines. Students who clear the portfolio before that fortnight have a materially easier DP2 than those who leave it inside it.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.subjectsIntro: CAS is organised in three strands and interacts with several Diploma subjects — including one rule that catches students out, because an experience cannot be counted twice.

subjects.name: Creativity
subjects.description: Arts and activities involving creative thinking, where the student is producing rather than consuming. Music lessons already taken, a school production, a design or coding build, a photography series. The usual gap is evidence: the activity happened and nothing records what the student initiated or how the work developed.

subjects.name: Activity
subjects.description: Physical exertion contributing to a healthy lifestyle. Club sport, swimming, martial arts, running, a training plan the student designed. Dubai families usually have this strand covered before DP1 starts, which makes it the cheapest place to evidence commitment and perseverance if the training is recorded as it happens.

subjects.name: Service
subjects.description: Collaborative, unpaid engagement with a community in response to an identified need, with a learning benefit for the student. This is the strand that stalls most often in Dubai, because a genuine need has to be identified rather than assumed and the organisation has to be one the school will accept.

subjects.name: The CAS project
subjects.description: A challenge of at least one month that involves collaboration and addresses one or more of the three strands, taken through investigation, preparation, action, reflection and demonstration. One month is a minimum, not a target, and a project designed in a week usually fails the collaboration requirement rather than the duration one.

subjects.name: Sports, Exercise and Health Science
subjects.description: Overlaps with the activity strand in content but not in credit: work assessed for a Diploma subject cannot also be submitted as a CAS experience. Students taking this subject often assume their practical work covers the strand, and coordinators rightly ask for something separate.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: The same double-counting rule applies. Studio work produced for the exhibition or the process portfolio belongs to the subject, not to creativity. A separate creative commitment — a community mural, a workshop run for younger students, an exhibition organised rather than entered — keeps the two clearly distinct.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Strong material for creativity provided the CAS experience is additional to assessed coursework. Running a drama club for primary students, stage-managing a production outside the course, or taking a show to a community venue all evidence initiative in a way a graded performance cannot.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Most Dubai students already have lessons, ensembles or a band, which covers creativity if recorded properly. The outcome that needs attention is usually new skills or perseverance: four years of grade examinations is commitment, and the portfolio needs to show what developed rather than that attendance continued.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: The engagement activity in this subject teaches exactly the investigate-and-act cycle CAS wants, which makes these students unusually good at designing a service project. The rule still holds: the engagement activity belongs to the subject and the CAS project has to be separate work.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: The two core components that carry marks, sharing a calendar with CAS. Worth listing here because the final CAS interview and the Extended Essay deadline usually land in the same term, and the component with no marks is the one that gets abandoned.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.regionsIntro: What stalls a CAS programme differs by area, because what is practically available differs. These notes describe what families in each part of the city actually run into.

regions.name: Jumeirah 1, 2 and 3
regions.note: Dense school provision and well-established CAS programmes with structured platforms and monthly checkpoints. Students here rarely lack activity or creativity; what they lack is service with an identified need rather than an afternoon at an event, which is what the final interview probes.

regions.name: Al Sufouh, Knowledge Village and Media City
regions.note: Proximity to universities and media organisations makes genuinely interesting creativity and service projects possible — workshops, mentoring, media production for a community organisation. The practical constraint is securing a named contact at an organisation the school accepts.

regions.name: Al Mizhar, Al Warqa and Mirdif
regions.note: Long-established schools with large cohorts and advisers carrying many students each. Portfolios here tend to be rich in experiences and thin in reflections, so an evidence-mapping session usually finds several outcomes already met but never recorded.

regions.name: The Sustainable City and Remraam
regions.note: Communities with their own environmental and community infrastructure, which produces some of the strongest CAS projects we see — a continuing commitment inside the community rather than a one-off event. The risk is a project that is organised for the student rather than by them.

regions.name: Dubai Sports City and Victory Heights
regions.note: Academies and clubs on the doorstep, so the activity strand is covered by default and often over-represented. These students need creativity and service deliberately planned, and the mentoring question is usually how to turn existing sport into a service commitment such as coaching younger players.

regions.name: Dubai South and Expo City
regions.note: Newer residential areas with longer journeys to the central school clusters, where weekday service commitments are hard to sustain. Projects that run at weekends or online, and that are properly documented, hold up better than ambitious weekday plans that lapse by November.

regions.name: Satwa and Al Karama
regions.note: Older, denser neighbourhoods near the centre with a mix of curricula. Many students here have genuine community involvement through family and neighbourhood networks that they do not think counts, and frequently it does once the need, the learning and the reflection are articulated.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches 2 and Mudon
regions.note: Villa communities with heavy HL loads and long school days. CAS here is usually the component with the least time, so the useful work is finding outcomes inside commitments the student already has rather than adding new ones in DP2.

schoolClusters.city: Al Sufouh, Knowledge Village and Dubai Media City
schoolClusters.note: Established Diploma cohorts close to the university and media cluster, which widens what a credible service or creativity commitment can look like. CAS systems here are generally structured, with the interview dates published in advance.

schoolClusters.city: Jumeirah and Satwa
schoolClusters.note: Long-running schools with strong co-curricular provision, so creativity and activity are usually well covered. The service strand and the one-month project are where students in this cluster most often need planning help.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Al Mizhar
schoolClusters.note: Large cohorts with advisers supporting many students at once. Portfolios from this cluster tend to be full of activity and short on recorded reflection, which an evidence-mapping session usually resolves quickly.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.modesIntro: CAS mentoring is short by design. These are the four shapes families in Dubai actually need, and the first one resolves most cases in a single session.

modes.title: Evidence mapping session
modes.description: One session that lists everything the student already does and maps it against the seven learning outcomes. Most students have met four or five outcomes without recording them, so the output is usually a short list of genuine gaps plus a set of reflections the student now knows to write. This is the session that resolves most CAS anxiety.

Each of the seven outcomes marked as evidenced, partly evidenced or missing
Double-counting with assessed coursework identified and separated
A written gap list the student can act on without further sessions

modes.title: CAS project design
modes.description: One or two sessions to design a project that satisfies the one-month duration and the collaboration requirement, and that the student can actually sustain. Work covers the investigation and preparation stages properly, because projects fail at planning rather than at execution.
bullets: A real identified need rather than an assumed one
Collaboration specified: who else, doing what, and when
Duration planned beyond the one-month minimum for safety
Demonstration planned at the start, not improvised at the end

modes.title: Reflection coaching
modes.description: A session on what a reflection has to contain to be worth the time: what happened, how the student responded, what they would do differently, and what they now understand about the outcome in question. Students write; the mentor questions and reads. Quality beats volume, and a portfolio of thirty thin entries is weaker than ten real ones.
bullets: The difference between a diary entry and a reflection, with examples
Reflections tied to named outcomes rather than written generically
Written at the time, not reconstructed months later
Every word the student's own, always

modes.title: Interview preparation
modes.description: Short preparation before one of the three documented interviews, particularly the final one. The mentor runs the questions a coordinator is likely to ask, checks the portfolio against the outcomes, and identifies anything that will be queried while there is still time to address it.
bullets: Portfolio checked outcome by outcome before the meeting
Likely coordinator questions rehearsed honestly
Gaps named plainly, including those that cannot now be filled
A short plan for the weeks between interview and completion

sections.heading: What CAS actually requires, and what it does not
paragraphs: CAS asks for four things. The student must engage in a range of experiences across creativity, activity and service over a period of at least eighteen months. They must provide evidence of having achieved all seven learning outcomes. They must complete a CAS project lasting at least one month that involves collaboration. And they must attend three documented interviews with the school's CAS coordinator or adviser, at the beginning, around the end of the first year, and at the end of the programme.

It does not ask for a number of hours. The hour requirement that older guidance quoted was removed, and nothing numerical replaced it. What replaced it is a reasonable balance across the three strands, judged by the coordinator, evidenced in the portfolio. This change is still working its way through conversations in Dubai staff rooms and family WhatsApp groups, and students continue to log hours as though the total were the deliverable. The total is not the deliverable; the evidence is.

It also does not ask for anything to be assessed. There is no mark, no grade and no moderation. The portfolio is not submitted to the IB for marking; it is the evidence the coordinator uses to determine that the requirement has been met. That is why CAS cannot be improved in the final month in the way an essay can. Evidence has to have accumulated while the experiences were happening, and a portfolio assembled retrospectively reads exactly like one assembled retrospectively.

What it does require, firmly, is completion. A student who does not complete CAS does not receive the Diploma, regardless of subject grades, TOK, or the Extended Essay. Every Dubai family should know that sentence by the end of the first term of DP1, because by DP2 the cost of learning it is measured in weeks that are already allocated elsewhere.
bullets: A minimum of eighteen months across creativity, activity and service
Evidence of all seven learning outcomes, not simply participation
A CAS project of at least one month involving collaboration
Three documented interviews with the coordinator or adviser
No hour requirement, no mark, no grade — but completion is compulsory

sections.heading: The seven learning outcomes and what counts as evidence
paragraphs: The seven outcomes are the whole specification, and most students have never read them in one place. They cover identifying strengths and areas for growth, taking on new challenges and developing new skills, initiating and planning an experience, showing commitment and perseverance, demonstrating the skills and benefits of working collaboratively, engaging with issues of global significance, and recognising and considering the ethics of choices and actions. A student must show evidence of all seven across their programme, not one each term.

Evidence is the word that does the work. Participation is not evidence of initiative, and attendance is not evidence of perseverance. What satisfies an outcome is a record showing the student doing the thing the outcome names: a plan they wrote before an event, a message chain showing them organising other people, a reflection written mid-commitment describing why they wanted to stop and did not. Photographs are weak evidence on their own, which surprises students, because a photograph shows presence rather than contribution.

In practice most students in Dubai have already met four or five outcomes through things they do anyway — club sport, music, a family volunteering commitment, a school council role — and recorded none of them against an outcome. One mapping session usually converts that into a short, specific gap list. The outcomes that genuinely need designing are almost always initiating and planning, engagement with global significance, and the ethics of choices and actions, because those three require deliberate thought rather than continued participation.

The outcome on ethics is the one coordinators probe hardest at the final interview and the one students answer worst. It does not require a moral essay. It requires the student to describe a decision they actually faced in a CAS experience — who benefited, who was excluded, whether the help offered was what was needed — and what they concluded. A real small example beats a general statement about the importance of ethics every time.

sections.heading: The CAS project: one month, collaboration, and where it stalls
paragraphs: The CAS project is the one structural requirement beyond the outcomes: a challenge of at least one month's duration that involves collaboration and addresses one or more strands. Students read that as a month-long activity and plan accordingly, which is why so many projects fail. A month is the minimum envelope, and inside it the project is supposed to pass through investigation, preparation, action, reflection and demonstration. Compressed into four weeks with no preparation, it becomes an event with a reflection attached.

Collaboration is the second trap. Working alongside other people is not collaboration; collaboration means a shared goal with interdependent roles, which produces the disagreement and negotiation the outcome is actually about. The projects that document collaboration well are the ones where someone had to be persuaded, a plan had to change, or a role had to be reassigned. A project where the student did everything and others attended is a solo project with witnesses.

The third failure is scope. Ambitious projects — a charity, a city-wide campaign, a fundraising target — generate impressive plans and stall on permissions, insurance, licensing and adult availability. In the UAE, community organisations and charities operate under licence and schools maintain their own lists of organisations they will accept, so a project requiring a new external partnership needs the school's approval before any time is invested. Ask the coordinator first; it takes one email and prevents a month of wasted effort.

What works in Dubai is usually smaller and continuing: a weekly coaching session for younger players at a club the student already belongs to, a sustained initiative inside a residential community, a skills workshop run repeatedly for the same group rather than once for an audience. These satisfy duration naturally, generate real collaboration, and produce reflections that have something in them.

sections.heading: Reflection that is worth writing, and reflection that pads a portfolio
paragraphs: Reflection is where CAS is won or lost, and it is also where students waste the most time. The IB does not require a reflection for every experience, and a portfolio of thirty short entries that each describe what happened is weaker than ten that show thinking. Volume is not the measure. What a coordinator is looking for is whether the student can describe what they did, how they responded, what changed as a result, and what they now understand about themselves or the issue.

The commonest failure is the diary entry: we met at four, we set up the tables, it went well, everyone enjoyed it. Nothing in that sentence evidences an outcome. The same experience reflected on properly says what the student expected, what actually happened, which part they found difficult and why, what they would do differently, and which of the seven outcomes the episode speaks to. That is four sentences longer and worth twenty entries of the first kind.

Timing matters more than form. A reflection written in the week it happened contains the detail and the uncertainty that make it credible; one written eight months later contains a summary and a conclusion. Coordinators read a great many of both and can tell them apart instantly. Reflections can be written, recorded as audio, kept as annotated photographs or logged on the school's platform — the format is the school's choice, and the timing is the student's responsibility.

One boundary applies without exception. Reflections are the student's own account of their own experience, and nobody else can supply them. A mentor may explain what a reflection needs to contain, ask the questions that produce the content, and read a draft and say which outcome it evidences. A mentor may not write reflections, and a portfolio describing experiences that did not happen is an academic honesty matter affecting the Diploma rather than a shortcut around a tedious requirement.

sections.heading: The eighteen months and the three interviews, counted from DP1
paragraphs: CAS runs for at least eighteen months and is punctuated by three documented interviews: one at the start, one around the end of DP1, and one at the end of the programme. Those three meetings are the only fixed points in the whole component, which means they are the structure a family can plan around. Ask for the dates at the start of DP1 — most Dubai schools set them per cohort and will share them on request.

The first interview establishes the starting point: strengths, areas for growth, and an initial plan across the three strands. Students treat it as a formality and it is the cheapest hour in the component, because an honest self-assessment at the start is itself evidence for the first outcome, and a plan written then is evidence of initiative. A student who arrives with nothing prepared has wasted the one meeting that could have shaped the two years.

The second, around the end of DP1, is the checkpoint that matters most. By then roughly half the eighteen months is gone and the gaps are visible: usually initiating and planning, global significance, and ethics. There is still a full year to address them, and addressing a gap in DP2 term one costs an afternoon rather than a crisis. Almost every CAS emergency we see in Dubai is a second interview whose findings were not acted on.

The third interview concludes the programme and is where the portfolio is reviewed against the seven outcomes. It typically lands in the same term as final examinations, the Extended Essay deadline and university decisions, which is precisely why the work should not be waiting for it. A student who walks into that meeting with each outcome evidenced is finished in twenty minutes.

sections.heading: Finding creativity, activity and service in Dubai without a dead end
paragraphs: The practical question Dubai parents ask is where the service comes from. Activity is rarely a problem here: clubs, academies, swimming and running are everywhere, and most students arrive in DP1 with the strand already covered. Creativity is usually covered too, through music lessons, drama, art or a build of some kind. Service is the strand that stalls, because a genuine community need has to be identified and the organisation has to be one the school will accept.

Start with the school rather than with a search engine. Coordinators maintain lists of organisations their students have worked with, and those relationships already carry whatever permissions and safeguarding arrangements the school requires. Community organisations and charities in the UAE operate under licence, and an unlicensed arrangement found independently can be refused however well-intentioned it is. One email to the coordinator before committing time saves the most common month of wasted effort we see.

The second route is the commitment the student already has. A swimmer who coaches a younger group, a musician who runs a weekly session at a community centre, a student who organises a recurring collection within their own residential community — each of these turns an existing activity into documented service with real collaboration. Service done with a group rather than for a group also produces much better reflection material, because the student has to negotiate rather than deliver.

Timing in the UAE has its own rhythm worth planning for. Community initiatives cluster around Ramadan and the national calendar, which makes those weeks productive for service and difficult for consistency, since school hours shorten and evenings move. Summer is long and many families travel, so a commitment that depends on weekly physical presence will break in July. Projects designed to survive both — with a defined end point and a documented handover — are the ones that hold up at the third interview.

sections.heading: The honesty line, and why CAS cannot be outsourced
paragraphs: Every part of CAS belongs to the student: the experiences, the evidence, the reflections and the account given at three documented interviews. There is no mark to inflate, which removes the usual incentive, and that makes the one real temptation starker — a portfolio describing experiences that did not take place, or reflections written by somebody else. That is an academic honesty matter, it affects the award of the Diploma, and the final interview is a conversation with a person who has read the portfolio.

The legitimate scope of mentoring is wide enough to be genuinely useful. A mentor can read the seven outcomes with a student and map what they already have. A mentor can explain what evidence satisfies initiating and planning, as opposed to joining. A mentor can design a project's investigation and preparation stages with the student, ask the questions that turn a diary entry into a reflection, and run the likely coordinator questions before an interview. None of that involves claiming an experience or writing a reflection.

This also shapes what we will not sell. CAS mentoring is short: an evidence-mapping session, perhaps a project design session, perhaps interview preparation. A provider offering a weekly CAS slot across DP2 is selling attendance, and a provider offering to build a portfolio is selling something worse. We say in the trial lesson when a family needs one session rather than six, and that is usually the honest answer.

On the regulatory side, private tutoring and mentoring in the UAE is permitted work. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through MoHRE; official guidance states it is granted free of charge for two years, with eligible applicants including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private tuition without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any quoted amount as unverified.

sections.heading: What CAS mentoring costs in Dubai, and when not to buy it
paragraphs: CAS support should be the cheapest core-component spend of the two years, because the useful version of it is measured in sessions rather than terms. For reference, the published Dubai market runs from roughly AED 45-65 an hour where EdFlik advertises and AED 33-52 at Tutopiya, through AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB at Unitors, AED 270 at TutorChase, AED 200-450 or above for specialist IB tuition in Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table, up to AED 650 for a premium named tutor at BartyED. Those are their published figures with their dates.

Against that, mentoring on outcomes and portfolio planning sits in the middle of the market rather than at the specialist end, because it does not require subject expertise — it requires someone who has run a CAS programme and knows what a coordinator asks. IB Gram does not publish a rate card here; a free trial lesson comes first, one per family and no card details taken, and the mentor's rate is confirmed in writing before any paid session.

There are three cases where we would tell a Dubai family not to buy anything. The first is a student whose school runs a structured CAS platform with monthly checkpoints and an attentive adviser; they already have the scaffolding and an outside mentor duplicates it. The second is a student in DP1 who simply needs to read the seven outcomes and start recording — that is a conversation at the kitchen table, not a paid session. The third is a student whose only gap is hours, which no longer exists as a requirement.

Where it does earn its cost is a DP2 student with a thin portfolio and a final interview approaching, a student whose project has stalled on permissions, or a student who has done a great deal and recorded almost none of it. One session can convert two years of real activity into evidenced outcomes, and that is the version of this service worth paying for.

sections.heading: Online mentoring against an in-home CAS tutor in Dubai
paragraphs: Dubai parents search for a home tutor, so the comparison belongs on the page even though CAS is the component where it matters least. An in-home tutor costs more per hour because travel is inside the rate — published bands put in-home one-to-one at roughly AED 180-350 against AED 150-300 for a qualified online hour — and for work that consists of reading a portfolio and asking questions, travel buys nothing.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Mentoring and tuition for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, and in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. We state it on every UAE page rather than letting a family discover it after a booking, because two providers in this market route UAE parents to numbers in another country without disclosing where their tutors are.

For CAS the online format fits the work exactly. The portfolio is already digital, usually on the school's own platform, so it sits on a shared screen with the seven outcomes beside it and gets mapped outcome by outcome. A project plan is built in a shared document the student keeps. Interview questions are rehearsed over video, which is also how a student will sound in a meeting. Nothing in the session requires anyone to be in the room, and the student retains everything produced.

The last practical point is scheduling. A single session booked in the week before a documented interview is worth more than a standing slot, and online delivery makes a one-off session at short notice straightforward rather than an imposition. Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time around the Dubai school day, with later evening and weekend-morning slots available during Ramadan and examination terms.

faqs.question: Is CAS graded, and does it affect my child's Diploma points?
faqs.answer: CAS carries no mark, no grade and no points. It is assessed only in the sense that the school's coordinator determines whether the requirements have been met, and the portfolio is not submitted to the IB for marking. What it does carry is a veto: completing CAS is a requirement for the award of the Diploma, so a student with strong subject grades and an incomplete CAS programme does not receive the Diploma. That combination — no upside, total downside — is why it gets deprioritised in DP1 and becomes urgent in DP2, usually in the same weeks as final examinations.

faqs.question: How many hours of CAS does my child actually need to do?
faqs.answer: None, in the sense of a target. The hour requirement older guidance referred to was removed and nothing numerical replaced it. What is required instead is a reasonable balance across creativity, activity and service over at least eighteen months, with evidence of all seven learning outcomes. Schools and parents in Dubai still occasionally quote the old figure, and the result is students logging attendance rather than building evidence. If your child's school sets its own expectation for time commitment, that is the school's requirement rather than the IB's, and it is worth asking which you are being held to.

faqs.question: What are the seven CAS learning outcomes?
faqs.answer: They cover identifying strengths and areas for growth; undertaking new challenges and developing new skills; initiating and planning an experience; showing commitment and perseverance; demonstrating the skills and benefits of working collaboratively; engaging with issues of global significance; and recognising and considering the ethics of choices and actions. A student must evidence all seven across the programme. Most Dubai students have already met four or five through commitments they hold anyway, without recording any of them against an outcome. The three that usually need deliberate design are initiating and planning, global significance, and ethics.

faqs.question: What counts as a CAS project and how long does it have to run?
faqs.answer: A CAS project is a challenge lasting at least one month that involves collaboration and addresses one or more of the three strands, taken through investigation, preparation, action, reflection and demonstration. One month is a minimum rather than a target, and projects compressed into exactly four weeks usually fail on collaboration instead of duration: working alongside other people is not the same as sharing a goal with interdependent roles. The projects that hold up tend to be smaller and continuing — a weekly coaching commitment, a repeated workshop, an initiative inside a community the student already belongs to.

faqs.question: How long does the CAS programme run for in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: A minimum of eighteen months, normally from the start of DP1 until the second half of DP2, punctuated by three documented interviews with the coordinator or adviser: one at the beginning, one around the end of DP1, and one at the end of the programme. The eighteen-month floor is the reason CAS cannot be rescued late — evidence has to have accumulated while the experiences were happening, and a portfolio assembled retrospectively reads exactly like one assembled retrospectively. Ask for the three interview dates at the start of DP1; they are the only fixed points in the component.

faqs.question: What happens if my child does not complete CAS?
faqs.answer: The Diploma is not awarded. Completion is a requirement independent of subject grades, Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay, so a strong candidate with an incomplete portfolio is in the same position as a weak one. In practice schools work hard to avoid this, which is what the three documented interviews are for — the second interview, around the end of DP1, exists precisely so gaps can be addressed while a year remains. The students who get into real difficulty are almost always those whose second interview identified gaps that were never acted on.

faqs.question: Can paid work count towards a CAS strand?
faqs.answer: Generally not. Service is defined as unpaid and collaborative engagement with a community in response to an identified need, and CAS experiences are not meant to be undertaken for personal financial gain. There can be nuance around work experience arrangements and internships, and the coordinator is the person who decides what their school accepts, so ask before building a strand around it. A more productive route for a student who is already working or coaching is to design a separate unpaid commitment that uses the same skills — the skill transfers even though the paid hours do not count.

faqs.question: Can my child's club sport outside school count for the activity strand?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in Dubai it usually does. Activity is physical exertion contributing to a healthy lifestyle, and training with a club, swimming squad or academy qualifies regardless of whether the school organised it. The gap is almost never the activity itself but the evidence: attendance over two years shows continuation, while the outcomes ask for new skills developed and perseverance through difficulty. A short reflection written during a hard training block, naming what the student wanted to stop doing and why they continued, is worth more than a year of logged sessions.

faqs.question: Does every CAS experience need its own written reflection?
faqs.answer: No, and the assumption that it does wastes a great deal of time. Reflection is required across the programme rather than per experience, and quality is the measure: ten entries that examine a response and a change are stronger evidence than thirty that describe what happened. A useful test is whether an entry says what the student expected, what actually happened, what they found difficult, and what they would do differently. Reflections can be written, recorded as audio or kept as annotated images, depending on what the school's platform accepts, and timing matters more than format.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my child with CAS reflections?
faqs.answer: A mentor can explain what a reflection needs to contain, ask the questions that produce the content, read a draft and say which of the seven outcomes it evidences. What nobody may do is supply the reflection, because it is the student's own account of their own experience and the coordinator will discuss it face to face at a documented interview. A portfolio describing experiences that did not happen, or written by somebody else, is an academic honesty matter affecting the award of the Diploma. The useful test is whether your child could discuss any entry unprepared.

faqs.question: How do we find service opportunities in Dubai that the school will accept?
faqs.answer: Start with the coordinator rather than with a search. Schools keep lists of organisations their students have worked with, and those arrangements already carry whatever permissions and safeguarding requirements the school applies. Community organisations and charities in the UAE operate under licence, so an arrangement found independently can be declined however well-intentioned it is. The second productive route is the commitment your child already holds: a swimmer coaching a younger group, a musician running a weekly session, a student organising something recurring inside their own residential community.

faqs.question: When do the three CAS interviews usually happen?
faqs.answer: The first falls in the opening weeks of DP1, the second around the end of DP1, and the third at the end of the programme, though each school sets its own dates per cohort. The first is the cheapest hour in the component and the most wasted: an honest self-assessment and an initial plan are themselves evidence for two of the outcomes. The second is the one that decides how DP2 goes, because it names the gaps while a year remains. The third reviews the portfolio against all seven outcomes and usually lands in examination term.

faqs.question: Does CAS make any difference to university applications?
faqs.answer: Not through points, since CAS carries none, but through content. A sustained commitment with a real role in it gives a student something specific to write about in a personal statement and something to discuss at interview, which a list of one-off events does not. Admissions readers see a great many general claims about teamwork and leadership, and very few concrete accounts of a decision someone actually had to make. The practical advice is the same as the IB's: depth over breadth, and keep the record while it is happening rather than reconstructing it during application season.

faqs.question: Can CAS continue during the summer holiday or while the family travels?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for Dubai families the long summer is one of the better windows for it, particularly for a project that needs concentrated preparation. Two cautions apply. Anything that depends on weekly physical presence in Dubai will break in July, so design a handover or a defined end point before the break rather than discovering the gap in September. And experiences undertaken abroad still need to meet the same requirements and be recorded the same way, so check with the coordinator whether the organisation involved is one the school will accept before committing the time.

faqs.question: How much does CAS mentoring cost in Dubai, and is it always worth it?
faqs.answer: It should be the smallest core-component spend of the two years. For reference, published Dubai market rates run from AED 45-65 an hour at EdFlik and AED 33-52 at Tutopiya, through AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB at Unitors, AED 270 at TutorChase, and AED 200-450 or above for specialist IB tuition in Bestimate's 2026 table. Portfolio and outcome mentoring sits mid-market rather than at the specialist end. It is not always worth buying: a DP1 student at a school with a structured platform and an attentive adviser already has the scaffolding, and we will say so.

The free trial lesson maps all seven outcomes and names which are evidenced, which are partly evidenced and which are missing. One trial per family, with no card details taken. For many Dubai families that single session is the whole engagement, and we would rather say so than sell a weekly slot for a component that carries no marks.

dubai/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: These specialists teach Chemistry at Higher Level: the three Structure strands, the three Reactivity strands, the Higher Level extensions in organic mechanisms, electrochemistry, entropy and transition metals, and the scientific investigation. intro.heading: Costing Higher Level Chemistry across two years, not one invoice
paragraphs: Most Dubai parents arrive at this search with the wrong unit of measurement. They ask what a chemistry tutor charges per hour, get a range from AED 150 to AED 650, and have no way to turn that into a decision. The useful question for Higher Level Chemistry is different: how many hours will two years actually need, and when in those two years will they be needed? Higher Level Chemistry is 240 taught hours against 150 at Standard Level, and that extra ninety hours is not spread evenly. It clusters in specific places, and so does the spending.

The shape of it is predictable enough to plan. DP1 runs mostly on foundations: the particulate model, bonding and structure, classification of matter, and the first pass at energetics and kinetics. Families who buy support in DP1 usually buy a little of it, steadily, to stop a gap compounding. DP2 is where the Higher Level extensions land, and where the bill rises: organic reaction mechanisms, spectroscopic identification using combined techniques, electrode potentials, entropy and Gibbs free energy, solubility equilibria, buffers, and transition-metal complexes. Then the scientific investigation takes its own block of hours, and then mock season takes another.

That pattern is why a flat monthly figure misleads. A family paying AED 800 a month every month for two years spends more than a family who buys four sessions in DP1 term two, a short block around the investigation, and a sustained run of weekly sessions through DP2 autumn and winter. The second family also gets better value, because their hours land where the Higher Level content actually is. The table further down this page sets out that phase budget in AED using published market bands, so you can build your own version of it.

The Higher Level premium itself is worth understanding rather than resenting. It exists for two reasons. Organic mechanism work and electrochemistry are genuinely harder to teach than stoichiometry, and fewer tutors do them well, so the pool is smaller and small pools price upward. And a Higher Level brief carries more marking: a Paper 2 extended-response answer on a multi-step mechanism takes real time to annotate properly, and a tutor who does not do that annotation is not giving you the diagnosis you are paying for. In the Dubai market an IB specialist sits at roughly AED 200 to 450 an hour, with Bestimate's published table at the same band and TutorChase quoting around AED 270.

One thing this page will not do is promise a tutor at a Dubai address. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Chemistry here is taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with mechanisms drawn live on a shared whiteboard and the annotated file saved for the student afterwards. For a subject built on curly arrows and reaction schemes, that saved file is a better revision artefact than a diagram on a kitchen-table notepad, and the specialist is chosen for knowing the current guide rather than for living twenty minutes away.

dubai/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Higher Level Chemistry is a Diploma subject, but the decision to take it is usually made a year earlier and the preparation starts there. The three programmes below are the routes Dubai students arrive from, with what each one leaves them short of.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Chemistry at Higher Level is one of the heavier Higher Level choices on content volume, assessed by two written papers and one internally marked scientific investigation. Students taking Chemistry HL alongside Biology HL and Mathematics are carrying three content-dense courses at once, and the practical consequence is a timetable problem as much as an academic one.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai, Higher Level Chemistry is most often taken by students heading towards medicine, dentistry, pharmacy or engineering, which means the grade carries admissions weight and the family's tolerance for a drifting 5 is low. Dubai schools run an August to June year, so the Higher Level extension content lands across the DP2 autumn and winter terms. That window is also when Extended Essay deadlines bite, which is why Dubai chemistry demand spikes in October and again in January.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Sciences is marked against four criteria rather than papers, with chemistry taught inside an integrated science course in most schools. Students come out able to design an investigation and evaluate a method, which is genuine preparation for the Diploma investigation, and without the stoichiometric fluency Higher Level assumes from week one. Mole calculations are the usual first gap.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run MYP straight into the Diploma with no IGCSE year, which makes the stoichiometry gap sharper here than in markets where every student sits a separate chemistry paper at 16. An ex-MYP student taking Chemistry HL in Dubai benefits most from four or five sessions early in DP1 on moles, concentration and limiting reagents, long before anyone mentions mechanisms.

programmes.name: IGCSE and the British route
programmes.description: Cambridge or Pearson IGCSE Chemistry to Year 11, then a split into A Level or the Diploma. A grade 8 or 9 in separate IGCSE Chemistry predicts a workable Higher Level start. A grade 6, or Combined Science rather than separate Chemistry, predicts a difficult DP1 and should change the decision about whether Higher Level is the right choice at all. Saying that early is cheaper than discovering it in February.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools carry the largest share of Dubai enrolment, so most of the emirate's Higher Level Chemistry cohort comes through IGCSE. The specific carry-over gap is quantitative: IGCSE rewards recall and short calculation, while Higher Level rewards multi-step reasoning with a data booklet in hand. Dubai students who scored highly at IGCSE and then slipped in DP1 have almost always hit that wall rather than a knowledge wall.

dubai/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Higher Level Chemistry is rarely the only brief in a Dubai household. The subjects below are the ones it is most often paired with, with what each assesses, so you can judge whether one specialist can carry two briefs and lower the combined bill.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Three Structure strands and three Reactivity strands across 240 taught hours, extended at Higher Level into organic mechanisms, spectroscopic identification, electrode potentials, entropy and Gibbs free energy, solubility and buffer equilibria, and transition-metal complexes. Two written papers plus the scientific investigation.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The same six strands at 150 taught hours without the Higher Level extensions. Mechanistic organic chemistry is much lighter and the quantitative equilibrium work stops short of buffers and solubility products. A sensible destination for a student whose DP1 Higher Level grade is not holding.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Unity and diversity, form and function, interaction and interdependence, continuity and change. The common Higher Level pairing for medicine applicants in Dubai. Shares the investigation format with Chemistry, so data-analysis coaching done once applies to both internal assessments.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Space, time and motion through to nuclear and quantum physics. Overlaps Chemistry at energetics, thermodynamics and atomic structure. Students taking both find the mathematical handling transfers; the command-term expectations do not, and that is where marks go.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Calculus, functions and algebra. Higher Level Chemistry leans on logarithms for pH and pKa work, on exponential relationships in kinetics, and on confident rearrangement throughout. A chemistry grade stuck at 5 is sometimes an algebra problem that chemistry hours cannot fix.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with technology. Workable alongside Chemistry HL, with one caveat worth checking early: some competitive science and engineering courses state a preference for Analysis and Approaches, so verify the requirement on the university's own admissions page before the subject choice is locked.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: An interdisciplinary course covering ecosystems, biodiversity, pollution and climate. Chosen by Dubai students who want a second science-adjacent subject without a second laboratory course, which leaves Chemistry HL as a standalone brief rather than part of a science pair.

subjects.name: Sports, Exercise and Health Science
subjects.description: Anatomy, physiology, energy systems and nutrition, with substantial biochemistry. Students taking it with Chemistry HL find the metabolic content mutually reinforcing, and the investigation skills are the same, which means one tutor can reasonably advise on both research questions.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Not a tutored subject in the usual sense, but the core components that collide with Chemistry HL in DP2. A chemistry Extended Essay needs a research question narrow enough to investigate and a supervisor relationship that the tutor supports rather than replaces.

dubai/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a Dubai family lives changes the timetable more than the teaching. The districts below are the ones that come up most for Higher Level Chemistry, with the specific scheduling fact that matters in each.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai
regions.note: Apartment living with short school runs to the central campuses and heavy evening road traffic at every exit. Families here favour a fixed early-evening slot and keep it, because a moved chemistry session in DP2 tends to become a cancelled one.

regions.name: Business Bay
regions.note: A working-parent district where both parents are often on calls until seven. Chemistry sessions here run later than the Dubai average, and the session note afterwards matters more because nobody in the household watched the lesson.

regions.name: Al Quoz
regions.note: A mixed industrial and residential area with several school campuses on its edges and an unusually wide spread of curricula in a small radius. A Higher Level chemistry student here is often the only one in their cohort taking it at that level.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Villa communities close to the Jumeirah school corridor, with a short run home and a genuine four-thirty start. The practical advantage is that a ninety-minute session fits before dinner rather than after it, which suits mechanism work needing concentration.

regions.name: Nad Al Sheba
regions.note: Spread-out villa plots served by a few large campuses, with a school bus that can run long. Chemistry families here frequently ask for a weekend morning slot instead of a weekday evening, and mechanism-heavy sessions do work better rested.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: A newer community with campuses inside it and a short walk or drive to school for many. Among the easiest districts in Dubai to run twice-weekly chemistry in, which is why Higher Level students here often buy two short sessions rather than one long one.

schoolClusters.city: Central Dubai and the Al Khail corridor
schoolClusters.note: The campuses serving Downtown, Business Bay, Nad Al Sheba and Dubai Hills families. Several run both a British route and the Diploma, so a Higher Level Chemistry set can be small, and a small set means fewer classmates to compare working with.

schoolClusters.city: Southern Dubai and the new communities
schoolClusters.note: Campuses serving Al Quoz, Al Barsha South, Al Furjan and the Sustainable City. A newer cluster where IB provision has expanded quickly, which is part of why specialist Higher Level science demand in Dubai has risen faster than supply.

sections.heading: A two-year Chemistry HL budget for a Dubai family, by phase
paragraphs: The table below is a planning instrument rather than a price list. It takes the published Dubai market bands for an IB specialist and maps them onto the eight phases of a Higher Level Chemistry course as Dubai schools actually sequence it, so you can see where the hours land and build your own forecast. The AED figures use the market band of roughly AED 200 to 450 an hour for an IB specialist, which is what Bestimate's rate table publishes and close to TutorChase's quoted AED 270.

Two features of the shape are worth noticing. The first is that the cheapest phases come first. DP1 term one and two need very few paid hours for most students, and the ones they do need are low-value in content terms and high-value in consequence: catching a stoichiometry gap in October is the single highest-return purchase in the whole two years. The second is that the expensive phases are short. DP2 autumn and winter carry the Higher Level extensions and the bulk of the spend, but that is roughly twenty weeks, not two years.

A family who follows this shape typically spends less in total than a family on a flat monthly retainer, and gets more useful hours. The retainer model charges you in July when nothing is happening and in February when everything is, at the same rate. The phase model concentrates money where the content is. What it requires from you is a willingness to buy nothing for stretches of DP1, which is harder than it sounds once a parent has decided that chemistry is a problem.

sections.heading: Where the Higher Level premium actually comes from
paragraphs: A Dubai parent quoted AED 380 an hour for Higher Level Chemistry and AED 220 for Standard Level is being asked to pay a seventy per cent premium, and deserves to know what it is for. It is not a surcharge for the word Higher. It is three specific things, each of which you can test in a trial lesson.

The first is content the tutor pool thins out on. Plenty of good tutors can teach bonding, stoichiometry and the first pass at energetics. Substantially fewer can teach a nucleophilic substitution mechanism properly, explain why a tertiary halide goes one route and a primary halide another, or walk a student through combining mass spectrometry, infrared and proton nuclear magnetic resonance data to identify an unknown. Fewer still handle electrode potentials and the entropy and Gibbs free energy material with confidence. Those are the Higher Level extensions, and they are where the premium lives.

The second is marking load. A Higher Level Paper 2 extended response on a multi-step mechanism cannot be marked usefully with a tick and a score. It needs annotation at the point where the student's arrow went to the wrong atom, which takes time between sessions that the hourly figure has to cover. The third is scarcity of the slot rather than the skill: Dubai Higher Level students want weekday evenings on Gulf Standard Time in the DP2 autumn term, and so does every other Higher Level student in the emirate. Ask a prospective tutor to teach you one mechanism in the trial lesson. The premium is either visible in that twenty minutes or it is not there.

sections.heading: What the two written papers reward, and where DP2 students leak marks
paragraphs: Under the science guides first assessed in 2025, Chemistry at Higher Level is assessed by two written papers and one internally marked scientific investigation, with no separate options paper. Paper 1 has a multiple-choice section and a data-based section. Paper 2 is short-answer and extended-response. Paper 1 carries 36% of the grade, Paper 2 carries 44%, and the investigation 20%. Check the detail against the guide your child's school is teaching, because schools moved to the current guides on different schedules.

The distribution tells you where an hour is worth most, and for Higher Level Chemistry the answer is nearly always Paper 2. It is the largest block of marks and the component where the examiner is reading reasoning rather than checking an answer. Students who know the chemistry and still score in the middle band are usually losing marks to presentation: a mechanism drawn without a formal charge, a curly arrow starting at an atom rather than at a bond or lone pair, an equilibrium answer that names the direction of shift without naming the reason, or an enthalpy calculation with the sign dropped.

The data booklet changes what is worth tutoring. Because constants, formulae and spectroscopic data are supplied in the examination, time spent memorising them is wasted time. What is not supplied is fluency in using them under pressure: finding the right table quickly, knowing which value the question needs, and not confusing two similarly named quantities. That is a drillable skill and it is cheap to buy. A tutor who spends sessions on recall that the booklet already provides is charging you for the wrong thing.

sections.heading: Comparing in-home chemistry tuition in Dubai with the online alternative
paragraphs: In-home tuition is widely sold in Dubai and the figures are public: Bestimate's table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour, independent home tutors quote up to AED 500, and monthly in-home blocks of four two-hour sessions appear at AED 1,599 to 1,799. Those numbers include a driver's time across a city where a cross-town run in the after-school window is rarely under forty minutes each way. The comparison below is between delivery models, not between brands, and it is specific to what Higher Level Chemistry needs.

Chemistry is an unusually good test case for this comparison because so much of the teaching is drawing. A mechanism explained verbally is forgotten; a mechanism drawn, annotated and saved can be revisited the night before the paper. On a shared whiteboard the drawing is already a file. On a kitchen table it is a page in a notebook that may or may not survive to May. For a sixteen or seventeen year old with a laptop, that is not a compromise relative to presence; for the specific demands of Higher Level organic chemistry it is a better record.

What in-home genuinely buys is the discipline of someone in the room, which matters for a younger child and matters much less for a Diploma student. What it costs beyond money is choice. A Dubai family hiring in-home selects from tutors who can reach their district inside the school-run window, and the set of people who can both do that and teach electrode potentials well is small. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE; our tutors do not travel to UAE addresses. If presence in the room is the requirement, a local in-home tutor is the correct purchase and we are not it.

sections.heading: The scientific investigation, and the line a paid tutor must not cross
paragraphs: Twenty per cent of the Higher Level Chemistry grade comes from one piece of individual research, marked internally by the school. It is the component where paid support delivers the most value per hour and where it most often goes wrong. The principle is not complicated: the report must be the student's own work in the student's own words, and the tutor's role is teaching and feedback. Crossing that line is malpractice under IB academic-honesty rules, and the penalty lands on the student's Diploma.

The legitimate work is substantial and specific. Most investigations fail at the research question rather than at the chemistry: a question that measures something already established produces a report with nothing to analyse, however neat the data. A tutor earns their fee by killing a weak question in week one and pressure-testing the replacement until it will generate a real relationship across a usable range. After that, the useful sessions are a mid-point check on whether the data collected can actually support analysis, and a reading of the draft that names where the evaluation is thin and where a conclusion has run ahead of its uncertainties.

What never happens in a session is text. A tutor does not supply sentences, does not rewrite paragraphs into better English, and does not hand over a method to be copied. Ask any prospective tutor what they do with a draft and listen carefully to the answer. There are providers in this market selling finished investigation reports at around AED 3,750. That is an academic-integrity breach, it is an IB malpractice trigger, and no amount of exam pressure makes it a sensible purchase.

sections.heading: KHDA, the permit, and what a Dubai inspection band does not tell you
paragraphs: Dubai's private schools are regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. KHDA inspects on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. That rating is a judgement about a whole school, and it is worth knowing before you draw conclusions from it: an Outstanding school can have a thin Higher Level Chemistry set with a teacher new to the current guide, and a Good school can have a chemistry department that has taught the Diploma for fifteen years. The band does not tell you whether your child's chemistry teaching is strong.

KHDA also confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there will be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for 2026-27, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. Separately, Dubai is adding seven private schools for 2026-27, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 places. More Diploma places means more competition for the same specialist evening slots, which is a supply fact with a pricing consequence.

On the tutoring side, the rules are federal. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without it are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published fine schedule, so treat any circulating amount as unverified. A tutoring business with premises in Dubai needs a separate KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, and no online platform should imply it holds one unless it does.

sections.heading: What a Dubai family should do if a year of spending has not moved the grade
paragraphs: This happens, and it is worth planning for before it does. A family buys weekly Higher Level Chemistry sessions through DP1, spends somewhere between AED 8,000 and AED 20,000 at market rates, and the school report still says 4. The instinct is to buy more hours. That is usually the wrong move, and it is the one most providers will encourage.

Four diagnoses cover most cases. The grade is not moving because the sessions are re-teaching content the student already understands, which feels productive and changes nothing; because the real gap is mathematical rather than chemical, so every chemistry hour is spent working around an algebra problem; because the student is not working between sessions, in which case weekly tuition is an expensive substitute for independent practice; or because Higher Level is genuinely the wrong level and the honest conversation is about moving to Standard Level. Only the first two are fixable by changing the tutoring.

The test is the marked work, not the feeling. Ask for the last four marked papers with annotations and look at where the marks were lost each time. If the same error recurs across all four, the sessions are not addressing it and the brief needs rewriting or the tutor needs changing. If the errors are different each time and the total is creeping up, it is working slowly and more hours may genuinely help. If there are no marked papers to look at, you have found the problem. We review at six weeks for exactly this reason, and we will say when stopping is the right answer.

sections.heading: If no Higher Level Chemistry specialist is free when you need one
paragraphs: Higher Level Chemistry in the DP2 autumn term, weekday evening, Gulf Standard Time: that is the single most contested booking in this market. Every Dubai Diploma family wants it, the specialists who teach mechanisms and electrochemistry well are a small group, and the slots are largely gone by February in an examination year. Most platforms handle this by taking the booking anyway and matching whoever is available. We would rather tell you the truth up front.

If a Higher Level Chemistry specialist is not free in your preferred slot, you get three honest options and no fourth. A different time in the same week. A weekend morning, which for mechanism work is often better anyway because the student is rested. Or a named date when a slot opens, with no payment taken until it does. If no specialist in a schedule that overlaps Gulf Standard Time covers the brief at all, we say so and state what we can offer instead, including the time difference, before you decide anything.

And if the honest answer is that we cannot staff the brief well, we say that. A Higher Level Chemistry student matched to a tutor who is confident on stoichiometry and vague on electrode potentials will have a pleasant term and no grade movement, and will conclude that tutoring does not work. That costs the family more than the fee. The practical defence is timing: settle this in the DP1 summer or the DP2 autumn, when choice is wide and rates sit at the bottom of the band, rather than in the final ten weeks when neither is true.

A brief that names the phase gets matched faster and quoted more accurately than one that says the student finds chemistry hard, because the phase determines which specialist skills the brief actually needs.

process.title: Use the free trial to test one mechanism
process.description: A full one-to-one session over live video at no cost. For Higher Level Chemistry, ask the tutor to teach one organic mechanism in it. Twenty minutes of that tells you more about whether the specialist premium is real than any profile does, and you keep the written diagnosis either way.

process.title: Build the phase plan, then the quote
process.description: After the trial, we map the hours onto the phases ahead rather than quoting a flat monthly figure: how many sessions before the investigation, how many through the extension content, how many for paper discipline. You see the shape of the two-year spend before agreeing to the first month of it.

process.title: Run weekly with annotated marking
process.description: A fixed Gulf Standard Time slot, a marked Paper 2 component in most sessions, and annotation at the point the reasoning went wrong rather than a score at the top. Mechanisms are drawn on a shared whiteboard and the file is saved for the student's revision.

process.title: Review at six weeks against the marked work
process.description: We look at the last marked papers together and ask whether the same error is recurring. If it is, the brief or the tutor changes. If the grade is moving, the frequency may drop. If the right answer is to stop, or to move to Standard Level, we will say so rather than selling another term.

whyPoints.description: Higher Level Chemistry spending is bursty because the content is. We map hours onto the phases where the Higher Level extensions actually land, which usually costs a Dubai family less in total than paying the same figure every month for twenty-four months.

whyPoints.description: A Higher Level Paper 2 answer marked with a number tells you nothing you did not know. Marked with annotation at the point the arrow went to the wrong atom, it tells you what the next session is for. That marking time is inside the rate.
