sections.heading: Mathematics, universities and the UAE equivalency layer
paragraphs: Families often assume Diploma Computer Science is the gatekeeper for a computing degree. Usually it is not. Most computer science programmes specify mathematics rather than computing, commonly Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and many will accept a student who never studied computing at school at all. The subject is valuable, and it is rarely the binding requirement. A student taking Standard Level mathematics and aiming at a competitive computing degree has a mathematics problem, and more Computer Science tuition will not fix it.

Inside the UAE there is an additional process to understand. The Ministry of Education operates certificate equivalency and the requirements differ by curriculum. On the British track, students must show five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. On the American track, English can be evidenced with IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in SAT reading and writing, and mathematics with at least 450 in SAT Mathematics.

For the IB specifically, no points threshold should be taken from a tutoring page. No IB equivalency figure in this project has been read on a Ministry of Education page, so the correct answer is to check moe.gov.ae or the emirate's attestation channel directly. Equivalency is completed by the family and the receiving institution. It is not something IB Gram performs, guarantees or speeds up, and tutoring is not a requirement for it. Any page implying otherwise is inventing urgency around a regulatory procedure that has its own published rules.

process.title: Confirm the course, the level and the option topic
process.description: Before anything else, settle three facts in writing: whether the subject is Computer Science or Digital Society, which level your child sits, and which option topic the department chose. Those three answers determine who can usefully teach your child, and getting them wrong is the most expensive mistake available in this subject.

process.title: A free diagnostic hour with a marked script and a documentation look
process.description: The first lesson is free, one per student, with no card details taken. It produces two things: a timed written question marked against the descriptors, and a short read of the solution documentation as it stands. Those two artefacts tell you which of the independent problems you actually have.

process.title: A written plan ordered by the calendar, with a total
process.description: The plan states which component comes first and why, how many sessions, how long each runs, and what the total comes to. In this subject the ordering follows the calendar rather than the weakest mark, because the case study and the solution both get dearer the later they start.

process.title: Review monthly, and stop when the plan is done
process.description: Each month brings the marked work and a short written note on what moved. If the marks are flat after six weeks of consistent attendance, the diagnosis was wrong and the plan changes or ends. Stopping costs nothing beyond the sessions taught, and plans in this subject should finish rather than renew indefinitely.

whyPoints.title: Priced against the published market, with the scarcity explained
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure here is attributed to the provider that published it. Three of the six pages competing for this search publish no price at all and two quote in US dollars, so there is nothing to compare a quote against. We also say why this subject prices high in Dubai, which is supply rather than difficulty.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the option topic, not on general programming ability
whyPoints.description: Because the school chooses the option, a tutor can be excellent and still be the wrong match. We confirm the option and the level before suggesting anybody, and if the person who fits is not free at your hour we say so rather than filling the slot with whoever is.

whyPoints.title: Documentation treated as the component it is
whyPoints.description: The marks students assume sit in the code largely sit in the planning, design, testing, recorded functionality and evaluation. Plans here state how many sessions go on documentation rather than on debugging, because a tutor who only improves the program is improving the part that is not directly assessed.

whyPoints.title: The keyboard stays with the student
whyPoints.description: Over video the student types and the tutor questions, which is the right way round for this subject and happens to be the honest one. We do not edit a student's files, supply blocks of code or take the keyboard, and sessions are recorded so it is clear who did what.

whyPoints.title: Online delivery, because the local pool for this subject is small
whyPoints.description: There are no home visits in the UAE. For a widely taught subject that is a convenience; for Diploma Computer Science it is the difference between choosing from the specialists willing to drive to your community and choosing from everyone who teaches the course at that hour.

faqs.question: Why does Computer Science cost more per hour than Biology or Economics in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Supply, not difficulty. Dubai had 227 private schools and seventeen curricula in 2024-25, with International Baccalaureate programmes taking roughly 7% of private enrolment, and Computer Science is an optional Group 4 choice inside that share. A school may run it with a handful of candidates across two years or not at all, so the number of people who have genuinely taught the course here is small. Published Dubai rates put specialist exam-year tuition at AED 200 to 450 and above on Bestimate's 2026 table, and this subject sits towards the top of that band for the same reason any scarce specialism does.

faqs.question: Is my child taking Computer Science or Digital Society?
faqs.answer: Check before hiring, because the courses need different tutors. Look at the subject name on the school report rather than what the lesson is called at home, then ask four questions: is a programming language in use and which one, is the internally assessed work a built product with documentation or a research inquiry, has the department chosen an option topic, and is there a Higher Level case study. Computer Science answers yes to the programming and the built product. Digital Society does not. Confirm with the Diploma coordinator in writing if there is any doubt at all.

faqs.question: Which component should we spend the first five hours on?
faqs.answer: Follow the calendar, not the lowest mark. For a Higher Level candidate whose case study has been published, those first hours belong there, because it is the cheapest component to prepare early and the dearest to prepare late. For a DP1 candidate the first hours belong to scoping the developed solution with a real client and writing testable success criteria, since a solution with an unworkable scope is the most expensive problem to discover in month four. For a DP2 candidate after the mocks, it is written-paper technique: pseudocode and hand-traced algorithms in the examination's own format.

faqs.question: How much of the Computer Science grade has nothing to do with writing code?
faqs.answer: A great deal of it, which is why strong programmers often underperform. The written papers examine system planning, computer organisation, networks, computational thinking and the chosen option topic, and much of that is answered in prose using syllabus vocabulary. The internally assessed component is marked substantially on documentation: planning, design decisions, testing, the recorded demonstration of functionality and the evaluation against the student's own criteria. Confirm the current weightings in the IB subject guide at ibo.org. The practical point stands regardless of the exact percentages: a plan that only improves the program is improving the part that is least directly assessed.

faqs.question: What should a tutor do when a program will not compile during a session?
faqs.answer: Ask questions and keep the student on the keyboard. A good tutor asks what the student expected, what the error message actually says, what they would check first, and then narrows the search by questioning rather than by reading the code aloud or taking control. The student makes every change and records the outcome in their own documentation during the session. What a tutor must not do is edit the student's files, paste in a working version, or tidy the code afterwards. Session recordings help here: they show exactly who did what, which protects the student as much as the parent.

faqs.question: What internet speed and setup does a coding lesson over video need?
faqs.answer: Less than families expect. A stable home connection anywhere in Dubai handles two-way screen sharing comfortably, and the practical requirements are a second screen or a reasonably large one, a wired keyboard the student is used to, and their own editor already installed and working. Headphones matter more than bandwidth, because a session of debugging involves a lot of precise talking. We ask that the project opens and runs before the session starts, since ten minutes of environment troubleshooting at a specialist rate is the least useful money in the plan.

faqs.question: How do we test a Computer Science tutor in a free first lesson?
faqs.answer: Ask for two things: a timed written question marked before the session, and a short read of the solution documentation as it currently stands. Then look at what comes back. A specialist names the band the written answer sits in, identifies which syllabus vocabulary was missing, and says which documentation sections will not earn credit as written. A general programmer comments on the quality of the code and suggests a package. The marked script and the documentation note also tell you which of the subject's independent problems you have, which is what determines the budget.

faqs.question: Is a university computing student a cheap substitute for a Diploma specialist?
faqs.answer: For one job, yes. A capable undergraduate at the AED 45 to 150 end of the Dubai market can teach a language, explain a data structure, and sit alongside a student debugging. What they generally cannot do is mark a long-answer question on system planning against the band descriptors, teach the examination's pseudocode conventions rather than a production language, or tell a student which parts of their documentation earn nothing. If your diagnosis is that the programming itself is weak, that tier is good value. If the problem is written-paper marks or documentation, it is a term spent on the wrong thing.

faqs.question: What does it cost to prepare for the Higher Level case study properly?
faqs.answer: Three to five sessions if started soon after publication, which at the AED 200 to 450 specialist band published for Dubai is roughly AED 600 to 2,250. Started in the final term it typically takes twice as long and competes with revision in five other subjects, so the same marks cost more and arrive less reliably. The work itself is independent research into a technical field: mapping the vocabulary and the underlying mechanisms, reading primary technical sources and citing them, then two timed extended responses marked against the descriptors. It is the most predictable purchase in Higher Level Computer Science.

faqs.question: Why do strong programmers lose marks on pseudocode questions?
faqs.answer: Because the examination uses its own notation and its own trace format, and fluency in Python is not fluency in either. A student who thinks in a modern language will write a correct algorithm in the wrong conventions, or will run a trace mentally and record only the final answer when the format requires every column filled at every step. Neither is a conceptual failure, which is why the repair is fast: hand-traced practice in the required format, marked, repeated. Six to ten hours spread across a term usually moves this part of the paper more than any other intervention available.

faqs.question: Should my child switch programming language to match the examination?
faqs.answer: No, because the written papers do not examine a specific production language. They use their own pseudocode, which has to be learned as a notation in its own right. For the developed solution the language should be whichever one the student can actually build and debug in, with the school's guidance, since a solution half-built in an unfamiliar language is a worse outcome than a complete one in a familiar language. The useful switch is not of language but of practice: traces and algorithm design done by hand, on paper, in the examination's format, rather than typed into an interpreter.

faqs.question: How many hours does solution documentation take to supervise?
faqs.answer: Four to six sessions placed at milestones rather than booked weekly. One to test the client and scope before a month is committed, one on success criteria that can actually be tested, one as a design review before development goes far, one or two reading the documentation against each criterion with the descriptor open, and one on the recorded functionality demonstration and the evaluation. Milestones rather than a standing slot, because solution work moves in bursts around school deadlines and a weekly booking bills you for the quiet weeks. The student writes every word of it; the tutor reads, questions and points at criteria.

faqs.question: Is a tutor worth paying for if the school has no Computer Science specialist?
faqs.answer: That is the situation where outside help changes the most, and it is not unusual in Dubai schools with small Group 4 cohorts. A student taught by a non-specialist is typically fine on whichever part of the course that teacher knows and thin on the rest, most often the option topic and the Higher Level extension content. The plan in that case is diagnostic first and broad second: find out what has actually been taught, then close the gaps in the order the calendar demands. Expect more hours than a student in a well-staffed department needs, and ask for a plan with a total.

faqs.question: Does a computing degree require Higher Level mathematics as well?
faqs.answer: Frequently yes, and more often than it requires Computer Science itself. Most computing programmes specify mathematics, commonly Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and many accept applicants who never studied computing at school. So a student taking Standard Level mathematics and aiming at a competitive computing degree has a mathematics problem, and additional Computer Science tuition will not solve it. Read the published entry requirements for the specific universities on your child's list before spending anything, then talk to the school's counsellor about the subject combination rather than about tutoring.

faqs.question: What happens to our plan if the option topic changes after we start?
faqs.answer: Schools very rarely change an option mid-course, but teaching staff do change, and with them sometimes the depth of coverage. If the option taught turns out not to be the one we planned around, the plan is rewritten and the hours move; you do not pay for sessions aimed at the wrong material. This is also why we ask for the option in writing from the coordinator at the start rather than relying on what a student believes it is. Mistaken option information is the most common cause of wasted revision in this subject.

faqs.question: What does a UAE university need to see from an IB student applying for computing?
faqs.answer: Two separate things: the university's own entry requirements, and Ministry of Education certificate equivalency. The requirements differ by curriculum, and the British-track rules are published: five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. For the IB, do not accept a points threshold from any tutoring site. Check moe.gov.ae or the emirate's attestation channel directly, because the figure circulating online has not been verified against a ministry source.

dubai/ib-dp-computer-science-tutor.closingHeading: Confirm the option, then buy fewer hours of the right person
dubai/ib-dp-computer-science-tutor.closingBody: If your child sits Diploma Computer Science at a Dubai school, start by confirming three things in writing: the subject, the level and the option topic the department teaches. Then take the free first lesson and ask for a marked written question and a short read of the solution documentation, because those two artefacts identify which problem you are actually paying to fix. One free lesson per student, no card details taken. Lessons run live and one-to-one over video on Gulf Standard Time, recorded, with screen sharing in both directions; there are no home visits in the UAE, and that service runs only in India.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Design Technology at Diploma level: human factors and ergonomics, resource management, modelling, innovation and the Higher Level extension topics, plus the design project from problem analysis through to testing. Sessions run one-to-one over live video with a shared screen.

intro.heading: Two different problems wearing the same name
paragraphs: Families who search for a Design Technology tutor in Dubai arrive with one of two situations, and conflating them wastes a term. In the first, the student is capable in the workshop, enjoys the subject, and is losing marks on written papers because Design Technology examines design as a body of knowledge rather than as a craft. In the second, the papers are fine and the design project has stalled — usually at problem analysis or at testing, which are the two stages students most reliably underestimate. These need different sessions, different materials and a different order of work.

The written papers catch students out because the subject is not what its name suggests to a sixteen-year-old. Design Technology asks about human factors and anthropometric data, about the properties of timber, metal, polymers and composites, about manufacturing processes and their economic scale, about the circular economy and green design, about physical and virtual modelling, and at Higher Level about user-centred design, sustainability, innovation and markets, and commercial production. A student who can build a beautiful product and cannot explain percentile ranges or the difference between batch and mass production will not do well in the papers.

The design project runs the other way. It is internally assessed and externally moderated, it carries a large share of the final grade, and it is assessed on documentation as much as on the artefact. Students lose marks there not because their prototype is poor but because the analysis does not justify the problem, the specification is unmeasurable, the conceptual designs are variations of one idea, or the testing is a photograph rather than a procedure. All four of those are fixable, and none of them requires anybody to touch the student's work.

On delivery, the position is set out before anything else. IB Gram teaches UAE students one-to-one over live video, with a shared screen for sketching, drawing conventions and CAD, and an annotated document the student keeps. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE; home visits are offered only in India. That matters more in this subject than in most, because part of Design Technology genuinely happens in a workshop. What a tutor can do about the workshop part is honest and limited, and the section on it says exactly where the limit falls.

What follows is built around the assessment: the components and what each one weights, the core and Higher Level topics with the question styles attached to them, the design project stage by stage, the drawing and CAD skills that transfer well over video and the ones that do not, and the academic-honesty position when the work being assessed is partly a physical object. Where a weighting or deadline is quoted, confirm it against the current subject guide through your school's Diploma coordinator, because guides are revised.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Design Technology students arrive from three different places, and the gap each of them has to close is specific. Knowing which one applies changes the first month of teaching entirely.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Design
programmes.description: MYP Design is assessed on four criteria — inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, evaluating — with no external paper anywhere in it. Students become genuinely fluent at documenting a design cycle, which is a real advantage going into the design project. What they have never done is answer a structured examination question about material properties or manufacturing scale under time pressure.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's continuum schools produce a steady stream of students who have done five years of MYP Design and arrive in DP1 expecting more of the same. The first term usually has to introduce the idea that two thirds of the Standard Level grade comes from papers about design knowledge, which is an unwelcome surprise if it lands in March of DP2 instead.

programmes.name: IGCSE Design and Technology
programmes.description: The British-curriculum route into the subject, with a written paper and a coursework element already familiar. These students have examination technique and workshop experience but meet entirely new content at Diploma level: anthropometrics in detail, the circular economy, virtual modelling, and the economics of production scale. The jump is in breadth rather than difficulty.
programmes.countryNote: The UK curriculum accounts for 37 per cent of Dubai private school enrolment, so IGCSE is the single commonest entry point into the Diploma in this emirate. Many Dubai schools run IGCSE to sixteen and then split into A Level or IB, which means a Design Technology cohort often contains both MYP and IGCSE backgrounds in the same room with opposite gaps.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Design Technology
programmes.description: Examined through written papers plus the internally assessed design project. Standard Level covers the core topics; Higher Level adds the extension on user-centred design, sustainability, innovation and markets, and commercial production, together with a third paper. The design project carries around forty per cent of the grade at both levels.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Design Technology cohorts are small, because the subject needs a workshop, a technician and a specialist teacher. A student may be one of very few taking it in their school, which means limited individual attention on the project and almost no peer group to compare documentation against. That isolation, rather than weak ability, is what brings most families to this search.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Design Technology sits next to a particular set of subjects on a Dubai Diploma timetable, and the overlaps are more useful than they look — several of them supply the exact knowledge the papers test.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Human factors and ergonomics, resource management and sustainable production, modelling, final production, innovation and design, classic design, plus the Higher Level extension. Marks are lost on command terms, on anthropometric detail, and on treating a design decision as obvious instead of justifying it against a specification.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Supplies the mechanics and material behaviour behind stress, strain, stiffness and structural choice. Students taking both find the material-properties content straightforward; students without physics need deliberate work on forces and on reading a stress-strain curve.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Percentiles, ranges, tolerances and scaling are all mathematics in disguise. Anthropometric questions are where this shows: a student who cannot interpret a percentile range will lose marks in ergonomics questions regardless of how good their design instinct is.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Shares drawing ability and critical vocabulary, and students often take both. The difference worth teaching explicitly is purpose: an arts drawing communicates intent, a design drawing communicates manufacture, and the two are marked on opposite criteria.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Useful alongside the modelling and virtual prototyping content, and the natural pairing for students heading towards product or interaction design. Shares the habit of iterating against a specification rather than designing by taste.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Directly relevant to the Higher Level innovation and markets content: market sectors, product life cycles, diffusion of innovation and the economics of production scale appear in both courses under different names.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Polymer structure, composites, corrosion and surface treatment make far more sense with chemistry behind them. Students without it tend to learn material properties as lists rather than as consequences of structure, which is brittle knowledge under examination.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Overlaps the sustainability, circular economy and life-cycle analysis content, and gives a student a second vocabulary for the green design material. A useful pairing for anyone taking the Higher Level sustainability topic seriously.

subjects.name: Design project support
subjects.description: Bought as a bounded block rather than a term: problem analysis, a measurable specification, conceptual design range, modelling strategy and a testing procedure that actually tests something. The artefact and the documentation stay the student's own throughout.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in Design Technology
subjects.description: Supervision practice rather than teaching: narrowing a question so it can be answered in four thousand words, and understanding what a supervisor may and may not do. Dubai supplies unusually good subject matter, from district cooling to desalination to building envelopes in extreme heat.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-home-tutor.regionsIntro: This subject needs materials, making and somewhere to photograph a prototype properly. Where a family lives in Dubai changes what is practically reachable, which in turn changes how a project should be scoped.

regions.name: Al Quoz
regions.note: Dubai's fabrication belt: print shops, acrylic and sheet suppliers, upholstery and metalwork units. A student scoping a project around laser-cut or sheet material can source and price it here, which makes a specification measurable rather than aspirational.

regions.name: Dubai Design District
regions.note: The emirate's design cluster, home to the Dubai Institute of Design and Innovation and a dense set of studios. Students here have real designers to interview for user research, which is the cheapest way to lift a problem analysis out of guesswork.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis
regions.note: Technology-focused community with a strong electronics and prototyping culture nearby. Projects involving sensors, microcontrollers or embedded electronics are easier to supply from here than from most of the emirate.

regions.name: Jebel Ali and Dubai Investments Park
regions.note: Industrial and port zone, which makes scale genuinely observable. A student writing about batch against mass production has actual plants within view rather than a textbook diagram, and that shows in a Higher Level answer.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Residential, with a long commute west towards the Al Barsha and Umm Suqeim school cluster. The sixteen hundred hour is lost to traffic here, so project sessions tend to sit in the evening when a student can have their sketches and models to hand.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Beach Residence
regions.note: Apartment living, which constrains making: no garage, no dust, limited storage for a prototype. Projects need scoping around that from the start, and digital modelling carries more of the load than it would for a villa family.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches and Dubai Hills
regions.note: Villas with garages and outdoor space, so physical modelling is practical at home. The common failure here is the opposite one: a prototype that gets built early and beautifully while the analysis and testing documentation stays thin.

regions.name: Dubai South and Expo City
regions.note: Newer communities with a built environment designed around sustainability and mobility, which is useful primary context for the circular economy and green design topics. Long distances from the older school cluster, so evening sessions are the norm.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai IB schools with established design provision
schoolClusters.note: Design Technology only runs where a school has a workshop, a technician and a specialist teacher, so provision is concentrated. Cohorts are small, which means a student's documentation is rarely compared against a peer's, and weak habits can go unchallenged until moderation.

schoolClusters.city: Newer campuses across southern Dubai
schoolClusters.note: Purpose-built facilities in the communities developed over the last decade, often with better making space than the older schools. The constraint here is usually teacher availability rather than equipment, and support tends to be bought for the project rather than for the papers.

sections.heading: What an online Design Technology tutor can and cannot do
paragraphs: This subject deserves a more careful answer about delivery than most, because a share of it genuinely happens with materials in hand. The honest division is this: everything assessed in the written papers, and almost everything assessed in the design project documentation, transfers cleanly to a shared screen. Cutting, joining, machining and finishing do not, and no video session will teach a student to use a band saw. Those are the school's workshop and the school's technician, and a good Dubai school supplies both.

What transfers better than families expect is the graphical work. Teaching sketching over a shared screen with both parties drawing is often clearer than standing behind a student, because the tutor's construction lines appear as they are drawn and the student can replay them. Orthographic and isometric conventions, dimensioning, exploded views, sectioning and tolerancing are all taught this way routinely. CAD is the same: the student shares their model and the tutor reads the feature tree, which is where most CAD problems actually live.

The project documentation is where online support is strongest, and that is fortunate, because the documentation is where the marks are. Problem analysis, a measurable specification, a genuinely divergent conceptual range, a modelling strategy, a testing procedure, and an evaluation that refers back to the specification line by line — all of it is written and drawn work that a specialist can read and interrogate. Most lost project marks are lost in those pages rather than in the prototype.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai, and there is no UAE office; home visits are available only in India. For a family that wants someone physically present in a workshop, the right answer is the school, or a local maker space, or an in-home agency in the emirate. For a family that wants someone who knows what a moderator looks for in a design project, distance is irrelevant and the subject specialist is what matters.

sections.heading: The components, and what share of the grade each carries
paragraphs: Design Technology is assessed through written papers plus the design project, and the balance between them surprises students who came from MYP Design. At Standard Level there are two papers and the project; at Higher Level a third paper is added covering the extension topics. The design project carries roughly forty per cent of the grade at both levels, which means the remaining sixty per cent at Standard Level comes from written knowledge about design rather than from designing anything.

Paper 1 is multiple choice across the core. It looks like the easy paper and it punishes vagueness ruthlessly, because a multiple-choice question about a manufacturing process gives no credit for general understanding. Students who revise by reading lose marks here; students who revise by answering questions do not. It is also the fastest component to improve, which makes it the right place to start when time is short.

Paper 2 carries structured questions, typically opening from a data or image stimulus and moving from short recall into extended response. This is where command terms decide outcomes. An answer that explains when the question said outline wastes time; an answer that states when the question said explain loses marks outright. Paper 3 at Higher Level does the same job for the extension topics and is frequently the weakest component on a Higher Level script, because the extension is taught late and revised less.

The table below sets the components against where marks actually go missing. Weightings are those commonly published for this course; confirm the current figures and the exact paper durations against the subject guide your school is teaching, through the Diploma coordinator. Guides are revised, and a tutoring website is not the right authority for an examination weighting.

sections.heading: The core topics and the question styles attached to them
paragraphs: The core runs across human factors and ergonomics, resource management and sustainable production, modelling, final production, innovation and design, and classic design. Each topic attracts a recognisable question style, and teaching the topic without the style is half a job. Human factors questions almost always involve anthropometric data and the interpretation of percentile ranges, which is why a student weak in handling data loses marks in what looks like a design question.

Resource management and sustainable production questions ask about material choice with a justification attached: properties, processing, cost, environmental consequence and end of life. The failure here is naming a material without naming why. Modelling questions ask for the purpose of a model — what it was built to test — and students who treat a model as a small version of the product rather than as an instrument lose the mark. Final production questions turn on scale: one-off, batch, mass and continuous production have different economics, different tooling and different tolerances, and examiners reward a student who knows which one a scenario implies.

Innovation and design asks about how products move from invention to market and why most do not, which requires named examples with real detail. Classic design is the topic students most often skip and the one that produces the easiest marks, because the criteria for calling something a classic are learnable and the examples are finite. A revision plan that leaves classic design until the final week is leaving marks on the table.

The table maps each core topic to its question style and the error that recurs. In sessions the sequence is always the same: teach the topic, answer questions in the style the paper uses, mark the answers against the command terms, then return to whatever the marking exposed. That is unglamorous and it is what moves a Design Technology grade.

sections.heading: The design project, stage by stage
paragraphs: The design project is assessed on documentation as much as on the object, and that is the single most useful thing a family can know about it. A student with a modest prototype and immaculate documentation generally outscores a student with an impressive prototype and thin documentation, because the criteria reward the reasoning. The stages are assessed in sequence, and each one depends on the one before it: a vague problem analysis produces an unmeasurable specification, which makes the conceptual designs unjustifiable and the testing meaningless.

Problem analysis is where the most marks are quietly lost. Students identify a problem they already have a solution for, then write analysis backwards to justify it. A moderator can see that immediately. Real analysis investigates the user, the context and the existing solutions, and produces findings the student did not know at the start. In Dubai that is an advantage rather than a chore: studios in the design district, fabrication units in Al Quoz and the specific constraints of building for extreme heat and humidity all give a student primary material nobody else has.

Specification is a technical skill and it is teachable in one session. Every line must be measurable, and a line that cannot be tested should not be in the document. Then testing becomes straightforward, because the test is simply the specification turned into a procedure. Students who write a vague specification in October spend March inventing tests for criteria that were never testable, and the evaluation reads as apology.

Conceptual design fails in a predictable way too: four concepts that are the same idea with different radii. Genuine divergence requires the student to design something they do not want to build, which feels wasteful and earns marks. Physical modelling needs a stated purpose per model. And the final evaluation has to return to the specification line by line, with evidence, including the lines that were not met. The table sets out what should exist at each stage and precisely where a tutor's role stops.

sections.heading: Drawing, CAD and the graphical marks nobody revises for
paragraphs: Graphical communication runs through every component of this subject and almost no student revises it deliberately. In the papers, a question may require a sketch that explains a mechanism or a modification, and marks go to clarity and convention rather than to artistry. In the project, drawings carry the reasoning: a well-dimensioned orthographic set shows a moderator that the student understands their own design, and a page of attractive renders with no dimensions shows the opposite.

The conventions are a short, finite list and they can be fixed in a few sessions. Orthographic projection with correct view arrangement. Isometric for assembly understanding. Exploded views for how parts relate. Sectioning for internal detail. Dimensioning that places each dimension once, on the view where the feature is clearest, with tolerances where they matter. Students who learn these stop producing drawings that are decorative and start producing drawings that are evidence.

CAD deserves separate treatment because the common problems are structural rather than aesthetic. A model built as a single lump of geometry cannot be modified, which means iteration becomes rebuilding and the student stops iterating. A feature tree with named, ordered, parametric features can be changed in a minute, and that is what allows a design to improve between drafts. Reading a student's feature tree over a shared screen is the fastest diagnosis available in this subject, and it is one of the few things that is genuinely easier online than in person.

Rendering is last and least. A photorealistic render of a product that has no dimensioned drawing behind it is a marketing image, not design documentation. Sessions treat presentation as communication: what does this image let a moderator understand that a drawing could not? Where the answer is nothing, the time goes somewhere else.

sections.heading: Higher Level: the third paper, and why it is usually the weakest
paragraphs: Higher Level adds the extension topics — user-centred design, sustainability, innovation and markets, and commercial production — and a third paper to examine them. On most Higher Level scripts this is the weakest component, for a structural reason rather than a conceptual one: the extension is taught in the second year, often compressed, and it arrives when the design project is consuming every spare hour. Students then revise the core they know and under-revise the extension they do not.

The content is not harder than the core; it is more abstract. User-centred design asks about involving users systematically in a development process, with named methods and a reason for choosing each. Sustainability moves beyond material choice into life-cycle thinking, the circular economy and the trade-offs between competing environmental objectives. Innovation and markets covers how products diffuse, why timing often beats quality, and what a product life cycle implies for a manufacturer. Commercial production covers the economics and the quality systems behind making at scale.

The question style rewards named examples with real detail, and Dubai supplies several. A city built in this climate makes life-cycle thinking concrete: district cooling, desalination, building envelopes, shading and the energy cost of comfort are all observable here rather than theoretical. Expo City and the sustainability-led communities offer design decisions a student can actually examine. A student who argues from what they have seen outperforms one who argues from a revision guide, every time.

The practical plan for Higher Level is therefore to start the extension early and deliberately, in parallel with the project rather than after it. Three or four sessions in the first term of DP2 on the extension topics, with question practice attached, does more for a Higher Level grade than the same hours spent polishing the core a month before papers. sections.heading: Academic honesty when part of the work is a physical object
paragraphs: Every subject has an honesty line; this one has a line that runs through a workshop, which makes it worth stating precisely. The design project must be the student's own work: their problem, their analysis, their concepts, their models, their prototype, their documentation. A tutor may teach a technique, explain what a criterion rewards, question a decision and give feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor may not supply concepts, write portfolio text, produce drawings for the submission, or build any part of a prototype. IB Gram does not sell finished coursework in any subject, and any provider offering to supply a completed design project is offering your child a malpractice case.

In this subject there is a second actor to be clear about: the technician. Workshop staff legitimately assist with machine operation and safety, and schools document that assistance. What matters for the student's mark is that the design decisions and the making record are theirs. Where a technician performed an operation, saying so in the documentation is the correct move and costs nothing — concealing it is what creates a problem.

A third practical point concerns photographic evidence. Moderators look for a continuous record of process: models at the stage they were made, decisions taken at the bench, failures as well as successes. That record is also, incidentally, the best protection a student has against any doubt about authorship. Students who photograph as they go have nothing to explain later; students who photograph a finished object have a conversation ahead of them.

The last point is about materials. IB, Cambridge and Pearson subject guides, past papers and mark schemes are copyright. No tutoring provider should be distributing them, and this one does not. Sessions work from the student's own school materials and from tasks written for them. Your school's Diploma coordinator can supply the current guide and the school's legitimate access to past papers.

sections.heading: Reading a Dubai school's design provision before you buy tutoring
paragraphs: Before paying anyone, it is worth establishing what the school already provides, because Design Technology provision varies more between Dubai schools than almost any other subject. The emirate's private schools are overseen by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, and KHDA inspects on a six-band scale running from Outstanding down to Very Weak. Those reports are published and they are more informative than any marketing page.

What to look for is specific. Does the school have a workshop and a technician, and is the subject taught by a specialist or by whoever was available? How many students are in the Diploma cohort, and does the teacher have time to read a project draft properly? Are there scheduled project checkpoints with feedback, or one deadline at the end? A school with strong provision and small classes may make tutoring unnecessary for the project and useful only for the papers. A school where the subject is taught alongside three others by one teacher is a different proposition.

The market context is worth knowing too. Dubai had 227 private schools serving 387,441 students in 2024-25 across seventeen curricula, with UK curriculum at 37 per cent of enrolment and IB programmes at 7 per cent. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees would not rise for 2026-27, and seven new private schools open for the 2026-27 intake, four UK curriculum and three IB, creating 16,846 new places. More IB places means more small Diploma cohorts in minority subjects, which is exactly the situation that drives families to look outside the school.

Two notes on what IB Gram is not. It holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE or IB accreditation and claims none; the regulators are named here so you know whose inspection report to read. And it has no UAE office or centre. A tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, which is a specific licence, and no online tutoring platform should imply it holds one.

process.title: Say which problem you have
process.description: Papers, project, or both. The two need different tutors' attention in a different order, and naming it in the first message saves a month. If you are unsure, send one marked paper and one page of the project portfolio and the answer becomes obvious quickly.

process.title: Send the school's project deadlines
process.description: Internal checkpoint dates matter more than anything else in planning this subject, because the project stages have to be supported before each deadline rather than after it. The Diploma coordinator holds those dates and they differ between Dubai schools.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: A full session with the proposed tutor at no cost and with no card details required. Bring a sketch or a CAD file and watch what happens to it. Within a session you will know whether this person reads design documentation the way a moderator does.

process.title: Fix the specification before anything else
process.description: If the project is the problem, the first real work is almost always the specification, because everything downstream depends on it being measurable. One session here routinely saves five later, and it is the cheapest intervention in the subject.

process.title: Separate paper work from project work
process.description: Alternate blocks rather than mixing both in one weekly hour. Paper work runs on a teach, test, mark, re-teach cycle; project work runs to the school's deadlines. Blending them tends to produce a term of pleasant conversation and no marked improvement.

process.title: Review the marked evidence at week four
process.description: Two marked scripts and one annotated portfolio section, read side by side. If the same errors are recurring with no movement, change the approach or the tutor rather than adding hours.

whyPoints.title: Taught against the assessment, not around it
whyPoints.description: Every topic is paired with the question style that examines it, and every session produces marked written work. Design Technology rewards precise knowledge about design, which is a different thing from being good at designing, and the teaching reflects that distinction.

whyPoints.title: Graphical work on a shared screen
whyPoints.description: Sketching, orthographic convention, dimensioning and CAD feature trees are all worked through live, with the tutor drawing alongside the student. Reading a model's feature tree over a shared screen is faster and clearer than looking over a shoulder.

whyPoints.title: Project support that respects the criteria
whyPoints.description: Stages are read in sequence, with feedback given as the questions a moderator would ask. Specifications get challenged line by line for measurability. The concepts, models, prototype and every word of the portfolio remain the student's own.

whyPoints.title: An honest account of what online cannot do
whyPoints.description: Machining, joining and finishing are the school's workshop and the school's technician. That is stated plainly rather than glossed over, because a family buying support for this subject deserves to know where the limit is before paying.

whyPoints.title: A specialist rather than the nearest available teacher
whyPoints.description: Design Technology cohorts in Dubai are small and specialist tutors are scarce. Removing distance from the shortlist means the constraint becomes availability in Gulf Standard Time rather than driving distance from your community.

whyPoints.title: Claims kept inside what can be evidenced
whyPoints.description: No regulator or board accreditation is claimed, because none is held. No grade promises. Weightings are flagged for confirmation against the current subject guide, and no IB examination date is restated from a secondary source.

faqs.question: Is Design Technology mostly making things, or mostly written work?
faqs.answer: Mostly written, which surprises nearly every student arriving from MYP Design. The design project carries around forty per cent of the grade and is itself assessed largely on documentation — analysis, specification, conceptual reasoning, modelling purpose, testing and evaluation. The rest comes from written papers about design knowledge: anthropometric data, material properties, manufacturing processes and scale, modelling, innovation and classic design. A student who loves the workshop and dislikes writing is in the hardest possible position in this subject, and that is exactly the gap one-to-one support is good at closing.

faqs.question: How can sketching and CAD be taught if the tutor is not in the room?
faqs.answer: Better than families expect, and in the case of CAD genuinely better than in person. Sketching is taught with both people drawing on a shared screen, so the tutor's construction lines appear as they are made and the student can replay them rather than watching once over a shoulder. For CAD, the student shares their model and the tutor reads the feature tree, which is where almost all CAD problems live: a model built as one lump of geometry cannot be modified, so iteration stops. What cannot be taught this way is machine operation, which belongs to the school workshop.

faqs.question: My son's prototype looks excellent but his predicted grade is low. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly the documentation. The project criteria reward the reasoning behind the object: whether the analysis justified the problem, whether the specification was measurable, whether the conceptual range genuinely diverged, what each model was built to test, and whether the evaluation returns to the specification honestly including the lines that were not met. A beautiful prototype with thin documentation scores below a modest prototype with complete documentation. The fix is reading the portfolio stage by stage against the criteria, which is work the student does and a specialist can direct.

faqs.question: What makes a design specification good enough to score well?
faqs.answer: Every line measurable, every line traceable to something the analysis found, and nothing in it that cannot later be tested. A line reading that the product should be comfortable earns little, because comfort is not measurable. A line specifying a grip diameter within a stated range for the fifth to ninety-fifth percentile of the target user group, derived from named anthropometric data, is testable and defensible. Writing the specification properly also makes the testing stage straightforward, because the test is the specification turned into a procedure. This is usually the single highest-value session in the whole project.

faqs.question: Which core topic do Dubai students most often neglect?
faqs.answer: Classic design, and it is the cheapest topic in the course to fix. Students treat it as general knowledge about famous products and leave it until the last week, when the criteria for calling something a classic are learnable in one session and the examples are finite. Human factors is a close second, but for a different reason: students assume it is intuitive, then meet a question with anthropometric data in it and discover that percentile reasoning is mathematics. Both topics reward a couple of deliberate sessions far more than another pass through material already half known.

faqs.question: How is Paper 3 different, and when should Higher Level students start it?
faqs.answer: Paper 3 examines the Higher Level extension: user-centred design, sustainability, innovation and markets, and commercial production. It is usually the weakest component on a Higher Level script for a structural reason — the extension is taught in the second year, often compressed, while the design project is consuming every spare hour. The practical answer is to start it in the first term of DP2 in parallel with the project, with three or four dedicated sessions and question practice attached. Front-loading the extension does more for a Higher Level grade than extra core revision in the final month.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the design project without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a line that is easy to state. A tutor may teach technique, explain what a criterion rewards, question a decision, and give feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor may not supply concepts, write portfolio text, produce submission drawings or build any part of a prototype. IB Gram does not sell finished coursework in any subject. Feedback arrives as questions in the margin, so the student revises their own work. Technician assistance in the workshop is legitimate and should be documented in the portfolio rather than concealed, which is the point families most often get wrong.

faqs.question: We live in an apartment in Dubai Marina with no space to build. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It shapes the project rather than preventing it. A student without a garage should scope towards work that can be modelled at a smaller scale, fabricated externally to a drawing, or carried further in digital modelling, with the physical prototype planned around the school workshop rather than the kitchen table. Al Quoz has print, acrylic and sheet-material suppliers who will cut to a drawing, which turns a space constraint into a procurement exercise and incidentally produces better dimensioned drawings. The projects that go wrong are the ones scoped without thinking about where making will physically happen.

faqs.question: Where can a Dubai student find users to interview for the analysis stage?
faqs.answer: Closer than most students assume, and this is where Dubai is genuinely useful. The design district houses studios and the Dubai Institute of Design and Innovation, Al Quoz is full of fabrication units whose staff know exactly why a design fails in production, and the building stock of a city at this temperature makes thermal comfort, shading and material degradation observable rather than theoretical. Primary research with two or three real users produces findings a student did not expect, which is precisely what the analysis criterion rewards and what a solution-first project can never fake.

faqs.question: Does Design Technology count as a science for university applications?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the university and the course, and it is a question to settle early rather than in the final year. Engineering, product design, architecture and industrial design programmes often welcome it; some engineering courses still specify physics and mathematics by name and will not accept design in place of either. The only reliable source is the admissions page of each named university and programme, read in the year of application, and your school's university counsellor handles this every cycle. Nobody should guess about an entry requirement, and a tutoring site is not an admissions authority.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a stalled design project usually need?
faqs.answer: Four to six, if they are placed correctly. The first establishes where the portfolio actually is against the criteria, which is often earlier than the student believes. The second usually rebuilds the specification so every line is measurable. The rest attach to the school's internal checkpoints: conceptual range, modelling purpose, testing procedure, evaluation. Beyond six sessions the returns fall sharply, because the remaining work is the student writing and making rather than anything a tutor can usefully add. Bounding the block in advance also keeps the spend predictable, which matters in a subject this late in the year.

faqs.question: Do we need a tutor who has taught the current subject guide?
faqs.answer: It matters more here than in most subjects, because guides are revised and this one has changed in structure before. Ask directly whether the tutor has taught the version your school is teaching and taken students through the design project under it. Then confirm the current weightings and criteria with your child's Diploma coordinator rather than relying on any website, including this one. A tutor working from an older guide will teach content that is broadly right and assessment advice that is subtly wrong, and assessment advice is most of what you are paying for.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover Design Technology and Physics together?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and the overlap is real. Forces, moments, stress and strain, material behaviour and energy all appear in both courses, and a student taking both tends to find the material-properties content in Design Technology straightforward. Pairing them with one teacher saves scheduling and means somebody notices when physics-style answers appear in a design question, which is a specific way to lose marks. Where it stops working is the project, which needs design-assessment experience rather than physics. Mention both subjects at first contact and the question of one tutor or two gets answered before any booking.

faqs.question: What do you do in the first session if the papers are the problem?
faqs.answer: Set and mark a short structured question set under time, then audit the core topics against it. That produces two things within an hour: a baseline mark on the record, and a list of core topics rated covered, thin or empty. The plan then follows the audit rather than the student's sense of what feels hard, because those two things usually differ. Paper 1 is normally the first target, since precise recall improves fastest and multiple choice gives no credit for general understanding. Every subsequent session ends with a task that gets marked before the next one.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send one portfolio page and one marked paper
dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-home-tutor.closingBody: The quickest way to find out what Design Technology support your child actually needs is to send two things: one marked written paper and one page of the design project portfolio. A specialist reading both will tell you within minutes whether the problem is command terms, core content, an unmeasurable specification or a conceptual range that never diverged — and those four problems have different fixes and different costs. Sessions run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, with sketching and CAD worked through on a shared screen. The concepts, the prototype and every word of the portfolio stay your child's own work, and the free trial lesson comes before any commitment.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-online-tut.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover Design Technology at Standard and Higher Level, along with the subjects Dubai DT students most often sit alongside it. Each match is made on evidence of having marked design-project work, not on a general claim to cover Group 6 and the sciences.

intro.heading: What progress in Design Technology actually looks like on paper
paragraphs: Design Technology is unusual among Diploma subjects in that a large part of the grade is visible months before the exams. The design project carries 40% of the result at both levels, and it exists as a folder a parent can look at. That makes it the easiest Diploma subject to hold a tutor accountable in, and the one where vague reporting is least excusable. A session that produced nothing you can see on a page produced nothing, and in this subject you can check that claim yourself rather than taking anyone's word for it. The folder is the receipt.

Dubai families usually arrive at this subject with one of two problems. The first is a strong maker who cannot write: the prototypes are good, the folder is thin, and the specification points are statements of intent rather than testable criteria. The second is a strong writer who has not made anything: the analysis is articulate, the development pages are decorative, and the testing section describes what would have happened. Those two students need opposite interventions, and telling them apart takes one folder review rather than a term of weekly sessions.

On the written side the evidence is equally concrete. Paper 1 is multiple choice and tells you almost nothing diagnostically beyond pace. Paper 2 is where the marks move, because its structured questions reward applying a core topic to an unfamiliar product rather than reciting the topic. Paper 3, which only Higher Level students sit, covers the extension topics and punishes students who treated user-centred design and commercial production as reading rather than as examinable content with its own vocabulary.

So the method on this page is deliberately unglamorous. Mark something real. Name the criterion or the question part. Write down what the next version must contain. Look at the next version. Dubai schools run tight internal deadline calendars for the design project, and a folder that moves one criterion a fortnight through the autumn of DP2 finishes in a different place from one that gets rewritten in a panic in February. Nobody can promise a grade, and a tutor who does is telling you something about themselves rather than about your child.

Delivery is fixed and worth stating early. Tuition for Dubai families runs online, one to one, over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run in-person lessons in Dubai, and home visits are a service we offer only in India. For Design Technology that turns out to suit the work: a folder is a file, a CAD model is a file, and a shared screen with both parties looking at the same page is a better review environment than two people leaning over one laptop at a kitchen table.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-online-tut.programmesIntro: Design Technology sits at the end of a design pathway that starts years earlier. These are the stages a Dubai student passes through, and what each leaves them able to evidence when the Diploma project begins.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme: Design Technology
programmes.description: A Group 4 subject built on six core topics covering human factors and ergonomics, resource management and sustainable production, modelling, final production, innovation and design, and classic design. Students sit written papers and complete one design project worth 40% of the grade, documented as a folder of analysis, conceptual design, development and testing. Higher Level adds four extension topics and a third paper. Standard and Higher Level are frequently taught in one mixed class in Dubai.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's design-project problem is rarely ability and usually workshop access. Schools vary widely in what their design suites hold, and a project that depends on a machine the school does not have stalls at development. A tutor's most useful early question in this emirate is which processes the student can genuinely reach, because the answer reshapes the whole project.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme: Design
programmes.description: MYP Design is assessed against four criteria: inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. That is close to the Diploma folder structure in miniature, and students who were marked honestly against MYP criterion B arrive in DP1 already able to justify a design decision rather than describe it. The habit that transfers best is writing specification points that can be measured.
programmes.countryNote: MYP cohorts in Dubai's IB World Schools are large, and the Design criteria are often marked generously at MYP 4 and 5. A student entering DP1 on the strength of an MYP 7 can still be a long way from Diploma standard on development pages, which is why the first folder review is usually more sobering than parents expect.

programmes.name: IGCSE Design and Technology as a feeder
programmes.description: Most Dubai DT students arrive from a British-track Year 11 rather than from MYP. Cambridge IGCSE Design and Technology (0445) and the Pearson equivalent both involve a coursework project with a design folder, so the format is familiar. What is not familiar is the Diploma's demand for commercial and sustainability reasoning, and for development pages that show iteration rather than presentation.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools account for the largest share of Dubai's private-school enrolment, so the typical DT candidate here has one coursework project behind them and a very different one ahead. The gap shows up first in analysis: IGCSE rewards identifying a need, while the Diploma expects a researched design opportunity with a named user group.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme: design and engineering pathways
programmes.description: A small number of UAE schools run the Career-related Programme, where DP courses sit alongside a career-related study in fields such as engineering, architecture or product design. CP students take the same Design Technology papers and complete the same design project. The scheduling pressure is different, because the reflective project and the design project compete for the same autumn weeks.
programmes.countryNote: CP provision in Dubai is thin compared with the full Diploma, so a CP student looking for Design Technology support is working in a smaller pool again. The practical consequence is that the weekly slot has to be fixed early; there is rarely a second specialist free to pick up a dropped session.

dubai/ib-dp-design-technology-online-tut.subjectsIntro: Design Technology students in Dubai tend to carry a particular cluster of other subjects. These are the ones we are most often asked to cover alongside it, with what each actually assesses so you can see where a shared tutor saves time and where it does not.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Papers plus a design project worth 40% of the grade. Marks are lost on untestable specification points, development pages that present rather than iterate, and testing sections written in the conditional. Higher Level adds four extension topics and a third paper on them.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The natural pairing for an engineering destination, and the subject that makes DT materials and structures content make sense. Mechanics, materials properties and energy transfer all reappear in the design project's testing pages, so one tutor covering both is a genuine efficiency.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The route most Dubai schools require for engineering and architecture. Heavy on algebraic technique and proof. A DT student whose maths is shaky usually produces weak quantitative testing, because they avoid measurements that need processing.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Stronger on statistics and modelling, which suits DT testing and user research directly. Students on this route find it easier to justify a sample of users or to handle survey data in the analysis phase of the design project.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Shares the solution-development logic with DT and is a frequent pairing for students heading towards product or interaction design. The internally assessed work falls in the same autumn window as the design project, so the calendar needs planning as one thing rather than two.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Chosen by DT students who want the drawing and making side developed further. Assessed entirely through a comparative study, a process portfolio and an exhibition, with no written exam, so the workload shape is the opposite of DT's and the two compete for the same evenings.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Underpins the materials and sustainable-production content in the DT core, and is required for most materials-science degrees. Carries the heaviest calculation load in Group 4, and usually needs its own specialist rather than being folded into DT sessions.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Overlaps the Higher Level extension topics on innovation and markets almost directly. Students taking both can have market analysis, product life cycles and target-market reasoning taught once and used in two subjects, which is one of the clearest overlaps in the Diploma.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The design project is marked partly on written justification, and students who cannot build a paragraph lose marks for the same reason in both subjects. Progress in written structure tends to appear in DT folder marks within a term.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: A design-based Extended Essay is tempting and often goes wrong, because students write a product review rather than a research question. A tutor can question scope and sources and give feedback on the student's own drafts; nothing beyond that is permissible.

sections.heading: What counts as evidence of progress in Design Technology
paragraphs: Parents are usually offered two kinds of reporting by tutors: a feeling and a grade prediction. Neither is evidence. In Design Technology there are four things that are, and all of them can be put in front of you. A marked script with the mark-scheme logic shown. A folder page with a criterion named against each comment. A specification point rewritten from an intention into a testable statement. And a version history that shows what the folder looked like six weeks ago.

The table below sets out what each kind of evidence can and cannot tell you, because they are not interchangeable. A Paper 1 score tells you about pace and little else; its multiple-choice format hides the reasoning. A folder page review tells you a great deal about the project and nothing about exam technique. Families who track only one of these are regularly surprised in May, when a strong project sits next to a weak Paper 2 and the final grade lands between them.

The practical standard worth holding a tutor to is this: after every session there should be a written note naming the criterion or the question part addressed, and one action for the student before the next session. That is not an administrative nicety. It is the only way to tell the difference between a term of teaching and a term of company, and in a subject where 40% of the grade is a document that accumulates slowly, the difference compounds.

sections.heading: The design project: criteria, and what a folder review changes
paragraphs: Forty per cent of the grade sits in the design project, and the criteria are published, which means the review can be mechanical rather than impressionistic. The project moves through analysis of a design opportunity, conceptual design, development of a detailed design, and testing and production, with Higher Level work extending further into commercial considerations. Confirm the current criterion letters, mark allocations and page limits with your school's IB coordinator, because guides are revised and planning around an old limit is an avoidable loss.

The single most productive review conversation concerns the specification. Students write specification points that cannot be tested: 'the product must be attractive to teenagers', 'it should be environmentally friendly', 'it must be easy to use'. Each of those is an intention. A testable version names a measurable quantity, a method and a threshold. Rewriting six specification points properly in one session changes the development pages, the testing pages and the evaluation, because every later criterion refers back to them.

The second is the difference between development and presentation. Development pages should show a decision being made: two options, a reason, a rejected route and why it was rejected. What students submit instead is a sequence of increasingly polished renders of the same idea. A folder of beautiful renders and no rejected concepts reads, to an examiner, as a project with no development at all, and no amount of drawing skill repairs it.

The third review conversation is about testing, and it has to happen before anything is built. Testing is marked on tests that refer back to specification points, carried out and recorded, with a judgement attached. Students who reach this stage with nothing measurable in their specification write testing pages in the conditional tense, describing what would be assessed if it could be. That is unmarkable. Scheduling the testing plan in the same fortnight as the specification rewrite is the one sequencing decision that saves the end of the project.

sections.heading: The written papers, and why Higher Level students lose Paper 3
paragraphs: Design Technology is examined through multiple-choice and structured papers, with Higher Level students sitting an additional paper on the four extension topics: user-centred design, sustainability, innovation and markets, and commercial production. The commonly published weightings put the design project at 40% at both levels, with the remaining 60% split across two papers at Standard Level and three at Higher Level. Confirm the current figures against the subject guide with your coordinator before building a revision plan around them.

Paper 1's multiple-choice format makes it the least diagnostic component in the subject. A student can score moderately well by recognising vocabulary and still not be able to apply a topic. Paper 2 is where that gap becomes visible, because its structured questions present an unfamiliar product and ask the student to reason about it using core content. Students who revised by rereading notes find they know the words and cannot do the task.

Paper 3 is the component Dubai Higher Level students most often underestimate, for a structural reason: the extension topics are usually taught late, in DP2, when the design project is consuming every spare hour. User-centred design has its own methodology vocabulary. Commercial production has process names students cannot bluff. Innovation and markets rewards reasoning about adoption and product life cycles rather than opinions about products. A short dedicated block on these four topics is frequently the highest-yield purchase an HL family makes.

There is a diagnostic shortcut worth knowing. Ask the student to explain the difference between a user-centred design method and a user survey, and to name two routes a product can take at end of life. A Higher Level student who has studied the extension topics answers both in a sentence each. One who has read the slides pauses, then describes a product they like. That two-minute test predicts Paper 3 performance better than any practice score, because the paper examines whether the vocabulary has been learned as content rather than absorbed as atmosphere.

sections.heading: Ten weeks of a folder review cycle, week by week
paragraphs: This is what an evidence-led block actually looks like across a Dubai autumn term, when the design project is live and the school's internal deadlines are approaching. The sequence matters more than the hours. Each week the student produces something, the tutor marks it against a named criterion, and the next week starts from the marked version rather than from a conversation about how it is going.

The cycle is deliberately front-loaded on analysis and specification, because everything downstream refers back to them. Weeks spent on analysis feel slow to a student who wants to start making, and they are the weeks that decide whether the testing section can exist at all. A project whose specification points cannot be measured arrives at testing with nothing to test, and that is a loss built in during week two that becomes visible in week nine.

A parent should be able to see this table working in their own child's folder. If week six arrives and there is still no documented rejected concept, the block is not working and the reason needs naming. If week eight produces tests that refer to specification points by number, it is working, whatever the eventual grade turns out to be. Nobody can promise where the mark lands. What can be promised is that the folder will contain evidence rather than assertion.

Two adjustments to the cycle are common in Dubai. Where the school's workshop time falls on a fixed day, reviews are moved to the day after it, so the student arrives with something made rather than something planned. And where a student is already at week seven with a week-three folder, the cycle is compressed rather than abandoned: specification and one documented rejection first, then a testing plan that uses whatever can still be measured. A compressed cycle scores; a skipped specification does not, however many weeks remain.
